subsubtopic: BENEFITS RELATED TO APPLICATION OF REGISTERED HOME OWNERSHIP SAVINGS PLAN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the latest budget, rules governing the use of Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans were changed. Not long ago, I pointed out that Canadian taxpayers will now be able to make tax-free withdrawals of any amount currently in their RHOSPs, for the purchase of furniture and household appliances. Another change is that Canadians who buy newly constructed homes after the date of the budget and before December 31, 1984, will be able to claim an additional deduction of up to $10,000. This means that if the taxpayer has contributed $3,000 to a RHOSP in previous years, he or she will be able to claim an additional deduction of $7,000 for the purchase of a newly constructed home, within the dates mentioned. The proceeds of the RHOSP must, of course, be used for the purchase of a newly constructed home and associated furnishings. Individuals must complete a written offer to purchase the home before December 31, 1984, with the date of closing of the purchase and occupancy no later than February 28, 1985. Homes for which a purchase agreement was entered into prior to April 20, 1983 will be eligible for the measure if the offer to purchase was signed prior to that date, provided the date of closing was not before that date.
I think that with the recent news about the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Plan, this measure provides a very satisfactory alternative to that program, as a substitute for the $3,000 offered to buyers of new homes.

subsubtopic: STATE OF EAST COAST INDUSTRY-COMPETITION FROM IMPORTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, for the past two years or more the East Coast fishing industry has been in the economic doldrums. This is an industry that is vital to more than 1,300 communities, over half of which depend
solely on fishing activities. It is the largest non-governmental employer in Atlantic Canada and Quebec, providing more jobs in absolute figures than does the automobile industry of Ontario.
In view of its importance to the nation, the Government established the Kirby Task Force to study the problems. Perhaps for the first time, fishermen, the unions, and processors realize that their adversaries are their competitors outside Canada. Americans are buying fresh cod delivered by air on a daily basis from Iceland, and Steinberg of Ottawa is selling frozen cod fish in one pound packages clearly marked as a product of the U.S.A. Obviously we are not only losing our foreign markets but our Canadian markets as well, and the key to our problem is quality.
New regulations call for all boats over 45 feet to carry ice, but this requirement has not been met. Bleeding and gutting as well as dockside grading are still local options. Fish holds should be upgraded to basic standards. Kirby also recommended additional ice-making facilities in coastal communities, but to date, this basic need has not been met.
Until we upgrade our quality, the improving fish markets of the world will be supplied by Iceland or Norway, or even by the United States. Therefore I urge the Minister and the Government to give a much higher priority to the basic needs of Canada's fishing industry.

subsubtopic: CONSEQUENCES OF ECON BANKRUPTCY FOR PRAIRIE FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it has been more than a year since Econ Consulting Limited of Winnipeg went bankrupt, leaving more than 300 prairie farmers out of pocket some $4 million. At the time of the bankruptcy in April 1982, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) refused to take the Canadian Grain Commission to task for the way in which it allowed Econ's directors to escape annual audits. He refused a similar request when it came to him from the National Farmers' Union.
As the Minister knows, 77 farmers have now launched a suit against the Canadian Grain Commission over the Econ bankruptcy. They are seeking the reimbursement of at least some of the money they lost when the company went bankrupt. Just a few weeks ago the Canadian Grain Commission's lawyers sought a stay of action in this suit. The judge hearing this case in Winnipeg has not yet ruled on the motion.

May 6, 1983
The universe is unfolding as it usually does when farmers in this country are being trampled upon. Thanks to the Canadian Grain Commission's lawyers, the lawsuit is stalled in the courts and western farmers affected by the collapse of Econ Consulting have still not been compensated for their losses.
When the NFU wrote to the Minister of Agriculture to ask for a public inquiry into the bankruptcy, the Minister wrote back to them saying that his Department had hired a consulting accounting firm to make recommendations about the Canadian Grain Commission's procedures. Has that consulting firm handed down its report yet, or was this pricey firm hired as a smokescreen?
We in the New Democratic Party have not forgotten about the Econ bankruptcy. We are watching and waiting to see what the Minister does to ensure that this will not happen
again.

subsubtopic: PLEA FOR WORLD PEACE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the ten-day visit of Pope John Paul II to Canada in September, 1984, will be an historic occasion, the first time that a Pope has come to this country where the Christian faith was planted so deeply more than 350 years ago.
It will not just be Catholics who will welcome Pope John Paul II. All Canadians of good will who recognize the Pope as a tireless promoter of peace and social justice throughout the world will rejoice to have him here.
When he spoke to the United Nations on October 2, 1979, Pope John Paul II said:
The Catholic Church in every place on earth proclaims a message of peace, prays for peace, educates for peace.
No issue before this Parliament, before any religious assembly, before the entire world, is more important today than securing peace through, first of all, ending the nuclear arms race. Canada must play a stronger role in the world community now searching for peace. Therefore I commend this vital theme of peace to the Pastoral Planning Committee organizing the Papal visit.
On behalf of the people of my own City of Edmonton, I also express the fervent wish that Pope John Paul include Edmonton in his cross-Canada itinerary.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ABOLITION OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in 1969 when the Government of Canada arrogated unto itself the exclusive monopoly on sales for freshwater fish in western and northern Canada, fishermen found that the Crown monopoly, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, was like a lobster trap. They were easily lured into it, but it was impossible to escape.
Despite subsidies from territorial and provincial Governments, the real return to fishermen has continued to decline since independent fish buyers were put out of business by the Government. What was once a thriving industry is now on the verge of collapse. The return to fishermen as a percentage of the final selling price is being reduced to a completely unacceptable level because of the inefficiency and ineffectiveness of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation.
Top quality Canadian whitefish, trout, and other species, should command premium prices on domestic and international markets, and fishermen should enjoy a high standard of living as a result of their labours. This will not happen until the fishery can be reorganized along free market principles and the stultifying bureaucratic monopoly of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation consigned to the garbage can of history.

subsubtopic: START OF WOMAN'S CROSS-CANADA RUN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the phrase "from sea to sea" will soon take on a new meaning for Kan-chan Stott of Ottawa. Kanchan starts her cross-Canada run from Victoria, British Columbia, today. When she reaches Halifax in October she will have established the longest distance ever run by a women. It is a run of epic proportions, but as well it is a feat which demonstrates the ever-growing contribution of women to sport and fitness in Canada. By this time next week, Kanchan anticipates she will have run 300 miles. We might keep that figure in mind as we contemplate what physical endeavours we should undertake for National Physical Activity Week.
Few Canadians are blessed with the requisite attributes and abilities of Kanchan to be champion marathoners, swimmers, or whatever. That is a fact of life for us to live with and should not deter anyone in the least from trying to improve their physical well being. No one has to earn a gold medal to become healthier or fitter; we just have to make physical activity a part of our daily routine.
Physical Activity Week is designed to encourage and challenge Canadians to put physical activity on their agenda. I hope Canadians take up that challenge and win their own personal awards.

subtopic: ADAPTATION OF SOCIETY TO SHORTER WORK WEEKS
ADAPTATION OF SOCIETY TO SHORTER WORK WEEKS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would address my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: ADAPTATION OF SOCIETY TO SHORTER WORK WEEKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that is a very good question. I would first like to say that, as part of the budget debate, I tabled a paper on employment perspectives in the 1980s which took into account both changes in population and growth of the labour market, as well as the change in the occupational structure, and the technological change being discussed, and analysed the consequences. I then put forward a four point strategy involving training, adjustment of workers to deal with job dislocation, direct employment programs to help people in high unemployment areas, and matters relating to the structural problems in the labour market.
We tabled that document with the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration which plans to hold special hearings, at which I will appear, and we are inviting other representation. In the meantime we have introduced programs like work sharing, which is designed to help people use their time when the job market is in decline or recession in different industries in order to be retrained during that period of time. We also established the ILAP Program which, again, is designed to deal with worker dislocation.
We recognize the fact that those changes are going on, but what we must also recognize is that the way to deal with them is through participation by business, labour and Government,

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance my question with regard to the over-all economic policies of the Government is directed to the Prime Minister. The unemployment statistics released today reveal that unemployment continues at 12.5 per cent. The Government's recent budget washed the Government's hands free of any direction for the over-all economy, and relied instead upon incentives to the private sector, at a time when we need a national strategy for economic development that will provide jobs for all. At the same time we know that one in every five young persons is unemployed although the same budget promised to meet the needs of young people. The dreams of young people have been shattered.
Does the Prime Minister really expect the people of this country to take seriously a budget which promised to meet the needs of young people, when one in every five young persons is unemployed?

May 6, 1983
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not believe that Members of this Government give up on young people as quickly and easily as Members of the New Democratic Party have obviously done. We recognize that there are difficult economic circumstances for young people because, as the job market begins to pick up, they are further back in the line as employers begin to hire workers who have been laid off or are out of work. At the same time the budget did address their needs in a number of very significant ways, first, by the Special Recovery Projects which will provide a major stimulus right across Canada, and many beneficiaries of these initiatives will be young people themselves coming into the job market.
As well, special funds were set aside for new youth strategy programs which are designed to break that framework of structural problems which young people face, through hiring people in the Department of National Defence, through Katimavik, and through working with the private sector.
The point about the budget is that, rather than relying upon one single magic fix which the New Democratic Party always tries to latch upon, this is a balanced budget.

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Say that again.

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It puts investments and commitments in a variety of areas, so that we work with the private sector, we work through direct employment programs, and we work by investing in human resource and training programs. That shows we have a proper balance rather than simply getting caught on extremes of the right or the left.

subsubtopic: YOUTH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the budget was clearly a supply-side budget. The Minister makes reference to funds in the budget for youth. If you divide the 600,000 young people who are unemployed into the $280 million promised for youth, you get $405 per unemployed youth over two years. Can that be a serious commitment to youth unemployment?

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. How can the Minister allocate in real dollar terms the same amount of money this summer as he did four years ago in 1979? Could he not take into account the fact that we are now in very different circumstances than we were four years ago, and will he not place a much higher priority on summer youth employment this year than he did four years ago?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the money being spent on summer youth employment this year is $170 million. That is up about 40 per cent over the expenditures we allocated in previous years. At the same time we have opened some 400 special youth employment offices across Canada to work with
the private sector to encourage not just big businesses but also people who work around their homes and in their small businesses to put job placements in those offices.
We recognize that as part of our approach to the problem we cannot do everything through Government. We can provide some leadership. We can help organize other sectors of the economy to try to tackle that youth problem. That is what we are trying to do. We are not trying to provide a monolithic one Government approach, but to work with all the other sectors of the economy, because we recognize it to be a national priority. Therefore we think that all Canadians should be working to get young people back on the job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL AID SOUGHT FOR POTATO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Agriculture. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL AID SOUGHT FOR POTATO PRODUCERS

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR HIGH TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my qustion is for the Minister of Economic Development. It is supplementary and it concerns unemployment, particularly as that affects young people. A couple of days ago the Science Council issued a report which stated that Canada is lagging far behind its competitors in the world in terms of funding for high technology industries. The Council mentions, for example, that the Minister has just announced the spending of $700 million over the next two years, while small European countries are spending billions of dollars on the development of high technology.
In view of the fact that some 21 per cent of our young people are unemployed, and in view of the fact they are very interested in advance technology, computers and micro-chips and so on, why are we so far behind our competitors in the world? Why do we not have more funding in terms of high technology development so there will be jobs for young people in the future in this country, as there will be in other countries around the world?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR HIGH TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, later today we will be having a debate on this subject. I hope the quality of the debate will surpass some of the questions asked, particularly those asked by the Tories. But the question of the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville is a thoughtful one.
I have had a brief look at the report of the Science Council. We have moved out on the issue of microelectronics in a very aggressive way with five major programs. We intend to continue in that direction. The $700 million that is referred to by the Hon. Member is, of course, incremental spending in this budget. There has never been such a thrust in the past. I

May 6, 1983
Oral Questions
suspect that very few countries have ever in their budgets come through with that kind of effort. It is exclusive, I might say, of tax incentives which are provided for and which will in fact be discussed by virtue of the White Paper which the Minister of Finance tabled with the budget.
I assure the Hon. Member that we are very conscious of the importance of training young people in microelectronics, not only through the programs which were detailed a few minutes ago by the Minister of Employment and Immigration, but also through our awareness program. We recognize that young Canadians in primary school and secondary school have to be aware of the opportunities that are being provided and will continue to be provided by these new technologies. That is part of the budget thrust. I would say that the effort is very substantial indeed. Perhaps we can take it up in more detail during the debate this afternoon.

Madam Speaker, the Government's Science Council says once again that, despite those programs, we are about four or five years behind some of the smaller European countries, let alone Japan. Last year in our country we had a net trade deficit of $8 billion in high technology, and by the year 1990 it will reach about $10 billion in computers alone. In light of that kind of information from the Government's own agency, can the Minister tell the House why he is not developing a policy to ensure that this viable industry will be Canadian owned? Otherwise, in the future the industry may indeed be very small, if it exists at all. We might instead be importing all of our high technology and equipment and, therefore, losing jobs for Canadians. What steps is the Government going to take to ensure that this industry will be Canadian owned and jobs will be created in this country for Canadian young people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government has always encouraged Canadian Ownership of many sectors, including high or advanced technology, and will continue to do so. It is interesting that the major players in this field in Canada are in fact Canadian owned and are world class. When the Hon. Member says we are behind, perhaps we are, but we are ahead in many other areas.
I remind the Hon. Member that, notwithstanding the abysmal rate of productivity increase in this country, the latest numbers out of the OECD show that Canada is still the second most productive, that is gross domestic product per worker, after the United States. Therefore we have a good base. Let us not lose it. That is what this technology program is all about. That is what this technology policy is designed to do, the policy which I tabled and spoke on earlier this week. From the comments we have heard from the Hon. Member, I judge that
he will be very supportive of the thrust of the policy which we are putting forward.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DUAL MEASUREMENT LABELLING OF FARM CHEMICALS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish to pose a question to the Minister of Agriculture. I would like to test the Minister on his statement that he is very easy to get along with. The Minister may recall that a few weeks ago I posed a question regarding dual labelling in metric and imperial of farm chemicals. He understands the problem. He has had representations from farm organizations. Has the Minister talked to his colleague who is responsible for metric, and has a decision been made to permit dual labelling of these farm chemicals?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR DUAL MEASUREMENT LABELLING OF FARM CHEMICALS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am fully aware of the debate on the subject of whether there should be dual labelling. A lot of chemicals used in Canada are imported. Therefore they have the American system of measurement. According to our discussions, this may create even more confusion. The Province of Ontario is sending out a guide for farmers to use so that they will not mix ingredients improperly for their spraying operations. I do not know of any decision having been taken on dual labelling. My officials in Agriculture Canada who have studied this have strongly advised against it.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT DISCUSSIONS BE HELD WITH FARM ORGANIZATIONS
REQUEST THAT DISCUSSIONS BE HELD WITH FARM ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, over the years this Minister has told us, time and again, that he is concerned about the farmers of Canada. Many representations have been made to him regarding this problem. He knows the feelings of the farmers and their problems. It is interesting to note that Gilles Cyr, a farmer in Prescott, Ontario, has published a book, on metric measurement of farm chemicals. He has received inquiries and orders for his book from all across Canada. If the Minister has the interest of the farmers at heart, surely he will discuss the matter with the farm organizations and with his colleague who is responsible for metric, and at least allow dual labelling so that farmers can carry on their farming operations without the danger of making a mistake when applying chemicals.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT DISCUSSIONS BE HELD WITH FARM ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is overemphasizing the situation and condition. I have met with many farm organizations and we have discussed this. I asked a number of these farm organizations whether they were concerned about it. Some have made no representations. They say their members have no concern, that they understand metric and are perfectly willing to use the metric system. Our statistics show there are not
May 6, 1983

more cases of misuse now than under the imperial system, when carrying out spraying operations.
The Hon. Member is trying to intimate that I do not care. I am as concerned as anyone. I am probably more concerned than he is. He is a great one at trying to make politics out of something and blowing it out of proportion, et cetera, for political gain. What he should be concerned about is the good of the agricultural industry and the fact that practically the whole world is using the metric system. There are only two small countries, Burundi and Nepal, I believe, that are not using the metric system. The Hon. Member would like to drag us back to the eighteenth century, or something like that.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S PROPOSAL TO RELEASE NON-VIOLENT FIRST-TIME OFFENDERS
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I have a question for the Solicitor General. He said that he wants to release first-time, non-violent offenders on earlier parole. Will the Minister tell us whether he includes under non-violent offences such matters as break and enter, theft, trafficking in heroin, and some types of robberies? Will he tell us what he means by the use of the term non-violent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S PROPOSAL TO RELEASE NON-VIOLENT FIRST-TIME OFFENDERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the first place the responsibility for release is not mine but that of the National Parole Board. I discovered that in a lot of cases where the Parole Board was releasing individuals it was not looking at the case at the earliest opportunity that it could under the law to do so. I indicated that I would like to see material submitted earlier to the Board by the parole service, which is under the responsibility of the Correctional Service of Canada, so that in those individual cases where it was prepared to release the non-violent offender earlier, it should have the opportunity to have the hearing to do so.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S PROPOSAL TO RELEASE NON-VIOLENT FIRST-TIME OFFENDERS
speechtext: In other words, the Minister does not wish to reply to the question.

Madam
Speaker, I would like to ask the Solicitor General whether he has ever met a victim of break-and-enter, a heroin addict, a victim of theft, a person who has been defrauded of their life's savings. Does the Minister include these matters as being violent or non-violent offences? Does the Minister think that a heroin trafficker should be let out at a sixth of his sentence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the offences the Hon. Member has described are nonviolent offences. Those are cases which I have asked the Parole Board to look at at an earlier opportunity. Of course, in the individual circumstances, risk to society does not only include the risk of re-offending, which of course a break-and-enter
Point of Order-Mr. Greenaway
artist has to be judged on as well as a drug addict or drug trafficker, but also the serious risk of the system of justice being brought into disrepute by people whose punishment requires that they be incarcerated longer, and their being allowed out before they should be. I think the Parole Board has statutory authority to look at the risk of society, not only of re-offending, which, of course, is within its mandate to do, but of bringing the system of justice into disrepute by allowing people out ealier than the sense of justice of the community requires.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to provide adequate and purposeful funding for Research and Development and specialized training, necessary to cope with technological change in the workplace which, according to a federal government study, will cause a serious displacement of jobs in manufacturing and business services, resulting in continuing high unemployment, forecast to reach fifteen (15) percent by 1991.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion we put down yesterday was in anticipation of the unemployment figures which were scheduled to be released today by Statistics Canada. If I can say this sarcastically, we were not disappointed because the figures released today indicated virtually no change in the unemployment rate month over month, and showed a substantial difference in the unemployment rate year over year. The unemployment rate today, according to Statistics Canada, is
12.5	per cent. That is up from 9.9 per cent seasonally adjusted for April of 1982. The fact is that there has been to change, seasonal adjustments notwithstanding. Given the fact that at this time of the year we would anticipate a sharp decline in unemployment, that means of course that there has been virtually a net increase in unemployment.
It is even more disturbing, Mr. Speaker, if you look behind the statistics. There is a danger of looking upon statistics merely as statistics and not in human terms. But if you look behind the figures, you will find some very alarming matters to which I will refer later in my speech. For example, there is a growth in the rate of long-term unemployment. There are a million people in Canada today who are classified as long-term unemployed. Next month there will be a million young people out of work. It is a very, very serious situation that we are faced with in this country today.
On Tuesday, May 3, 1983, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) outlined four main objectives of the Government's new technological policy. These were: First, to strengthen the Canadian economy through the development of new technologies for producing goods and services and the widespread adoption of new and existing
May 6, 1983

technologies. Second, to manage the process of technological development so as to ensure that Canadians are aware of both the opportunities and the problems that might arise. Third, to ensure that the benefits to technological development are shared equitably among all Canadians in every region. Fourth to create a social climate that places a premium on scientific and technological excellence, curiosity, and innovation.
In layman's terms, we are seeing that the Government is finally coming to grips with reality, the reality being that it has not provided the kind of leadership that would speak to the need for the new forms of training and new kinds of social adjustment needed to cope with the new technology as we enter into the micro-chip society. Let me quote the following:
Canada faces the strong likelihood of sustained unemployment with the associated problems of alcoholism, crime, vandalism and family breakups. Young people will be particularly hard hit and the disparity between the rich and poor regions in Canada is likely to increase.
I did not say that. The Bishops said as much, but that is what one would expect the church to say. That is what one would expect the Canadian Council on Social Development to say. That statement came from a report commisioned by the Ministry of State for Economic Development, a report which was leaked to the Globe and Mail.
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is what this debate is all about, because if we fail to recognize the changes in our society as a result of the new high technology, very serious social problems will be created down the road. Indeed, because of the number of long-term unemployed in this country, I predict that we may be very close to such a situation. As we enter into the heat of the summer, the situation will heat up and we could very well have violence on the streets, although I pray to God that that will hot happen.
The Minister of State responsible for economic development tries to tell us that all is well, but in actual fact we see the Minister, who has a leadership role, and his colleagues closing their eyes to the reality of the situation by failing to face up to the facts contained not only in the study to which I just referred but in other studies by experts within and without the Government who have tried to warn the Government what to expect.
The sad fact is that Canada is not ready for this new age. Canada is not ready for this new industrial revolution, this new micro-chip society. As a sad consequence, we are told by the Government, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and by Government studies that we must condition ourselves to double-digit unemployment. Indeed double-digit unemployment is here to stay. The report to which I just referred, the one commissioned by the Ministry of State for Economic Development, talked about unemployment reaching 15 per cent by 1991.
What does this mean? It means that the Government is now gearing its policy to that fact because it has accepted it. It hopes that by the extension of double-digit unemployment month after month Canadians will become conditioned to it. The Government has doomed a large segment of the population to the stigma of being unemployable. We have heard
Supply
about the untouchables in other societies. We now have the unemployables in our society. These are people who are unemployable because they are the long-term unemployed, the chronically unemployed, the discouraged unemployed and the untrained unemployed. I cannot accept and refuse to accept that as a fact of Canadian life. I for one, and indeed the people of the country, expect the Government to provide some form of leadership to deal with that situation, with this new phenomenon of Canadian life.
I am sorry to say that we had evidence of lack of leadership today in the House. We see day after day that leadership is not forthcoming. Consequently, a large segment of our population is doomed to being unemployable. That is what The Globe and Mail carried in its story of the leaked document commissioned by the Ministry of State for Economic Development which dramatically underlined the problem.
All we have to do is to look at the unemployment statistics. Anyone who tries to draw any consolation or satisfaction from the unemployment statistics released today is whistling in the dark and failing to face up to reality. As I have indicated, the minute decline in the seasonally-adjusted rate means that there has been no change in the rate of unemployment. In fact, there has been a net increase in the rate of unemployment when it should be going down.
Let us take a look at the unemployment situation. Let us go behind the statistics because behind them is the potential for human tragedy. Behind every one of these statistics is a human being, a Canadian who faces the prospect of having no job. Unemployment for women is up by 23.2 per cent over April, 1982. In 1982 we were supposed to be in the depths of the recession, yet we see an increase today over 1982 of 23.2 per cent in unemployment among women. There are 609,000 women in the country who are unemployed today. That is unacceptable. Youth unemployment is up by 21.8 per cent from April, 1982. Today there are 624,000 young people between the ages of 15 and 24 without job prospects. They are soon to be joined by an army of young people coming from our universities and post-secondary institutions looking for jobs and having no job prospects. The lack of prospects of a million young people in our country causes me to be ashamed.
Let us take a look at the long-term unemployed because they represent the core of the unemployables. This is what speaks to the recommendations contained in the various reports tabled in the House. It was referred to by the Ministry of State for Economic Development and in the report released by the Science Council of Canada. Long-term unemployed is up by 62.5 per cent over April, 1982. These are people who have been unemployed 3.5 months or more. Today, 931,000 Canadians have been unemployed for 3.5 months or more. Most of them have seen their Unemployment Insurance benefits expire. All these facts are coming from the catalogue released by Statistics Canada today. If we add to that the 118,000-and that is in there-discouraged workers, those who have given up looking for jobs because the prospects are

May 6, 1983
Supply
not there, we have a million people who constitute the vast army of unemployables in Canada today. These are people who have given up because there are no job prospects. I know what I speak of because I come from an area where this is a well-known fact of life, where chronically high unemployment has been rampant for so long that large segments of the work force have given up looking for jobs because there are in fact no job prospects.
That is the situation in Canada today as we head into the era of the new industrial revolution, the micro-chip society. That is the situation which cries out for leadership. That is the situation the Government has failed to address, both in terms of its response in the House, as exemplified by the statements yesterday of Minister of State for Economic Development, and in terms of its response in the budget. That is the situation which we as a Party are trying to highlight in the House today in the debate on the motion before us. This is the product of years of shortsightedness and neglect by a Government which tends to hide its head in the sand when all danger signals are in front of it.
Let us take a look at the record. We heard from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) today, but let me first indicate that the emphasis must be on employment training as we head into the era of high technology. In the five-year period from 1976-77 to 1981-82, the federal Government's investment in employment training in constant dollars dropped every year except for the one year when there was a change in Government. That year it rose by 5 per cent; when this Party was in power, money for manpower training programs rose by 5 per cent. Between 1976-77 and 1982-83 real spending on employment training actually dropped by 13 per cent, whereas total Government spending rose in real terms during the same period of time. The first year when real employment training expenditures rose under the Liberal Government since 1976 was the year i982-8 j. Finally, there is a recognition that the Government has not put enough emphasis on the right kinds of training programs.
Let me now take a look at the Government's record in terms of research and development. We all know that it is an appalling record. We are paying for the lack of emphasis on research and development right now by the staggering rate of unemployment and by the prospects of double-digit unemployment well into the 1980s. That is the cost of the failure of the Government to give adequate or sufficient priority to research and development. Last year research and development expenditures in Canada accounted for 1.3 per cent of GNP, the same level as they were in 1976, the growth in the economy, the technological changes in the work force and the marketplace notwithstanding. The federal Government's share of the spending has dropped from 47 per cent in the period from 1963 to 1967 to 33 per cent this year. This means that the federal Government has transferred the burden of funding for research and development to the private sector and to educational institutions.
The leadership, which should be coming from the Govern-I ment of Canada, has been abdicated in the hope that it will be taken up by the private sector and by educational institutions.
As a consequence, surely our situation today should come as no surprise. We have failed to invest in those areas which we know from experience promote higher real growth, the rate of productivity and an enhanced competitive position in world markets. That is the consequence we are facing today. Without such investment, our recent job losses were and are inevitable. We lost 7,000 jobs in one month in the manufacturing sector. That is a situation which, I predict, will continue. By failing to invest adequately over the years in research and development we have failed to provide the seeds necessary to ensure a good harvest. The young people of this country, the women of this country, are the ones who are paying for that fact. Wayne Simpson, an economist at the University of Manitoba, stated in a study which was commissioned by the Economic Council of Canada that the challenge facing Canadian policymakers since the early 1970s has been defined as non-inflationary solutions to high unemployment and low productivity. He goes on to observe, and I quote:
Effective training to eliminate observed deficiencies of skilled labour may simultaneously raise productivity, reduce inflation and lower unemployment. In short, it can help to solve three major problems facing the Canadian economy today.
Of course, the same observations apply equally to research and development. The Government, Mr. Speaker, thus stands condemned for its failure to recognize that investment in these two areas represents our best hope of promoting non-inflationary economic growth and high levels of employment.
Who are the first to be fired and the last to be hired in a recession? The first to go are the women, the young people, the disadvantaged, the ethnic groups, the native people. They are the first to be fired in a recession. They are the last to be rehired in times of economic recovery. Unless something is done for these people, they will constitute the unemployable of our society as we head into the micro-chip society. Who provides the majority of the work in our service sector, in the offices across the country? Women. These jobs will disappear as a consequence of the new technology. These are the women for whom we have been striving to provide equality of opportunity in the workplace by affirmative action and other programs and who will be doomed to having no job prospects. There will be no work for them. They will not be able to help feed their families. If they happen to be the heads of families, they will be doomed to welfare.
That is the consequence of the failure of this Government to provide leadership, to listen to its own experts, to read the signs which are there as we head out of the recession into the micro-chip society. We now have a Government which has, as a part of its economic recovery, a recognition that double-digit unemployment is going to be here for the rest of the decade. In fact, according to its own projections, unemployment will rise to 15 per cent by 1991. That is a disgraceful fact and one that is not acceptable to the people of Canada. It is one which represents, in my view, a total abdication of leadership on the part of this Government.
May 6, 1983

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to engage in this debate and I thank my colleague from the Tory Party for bringing forward the matter of technological change to be debated today in this House. The choice of technological change, as a topic for debate in this House is right on target because today the unemployment statistics came out once again, and while, to be fair to the Government, the level of unemployment in terms of percentages is down marginally, the over-all picture with regard to unemployment in this country has remained the same. Unemployment is at the 12 per cent level, which is very high, and the budget recognized this and pointed it out. These are levels which are unacceptable to Canadians.
Technological change is going to continue to threaten the employment prospects of Canadians. Therefore, these two topics, unemployment and technological change, go hand in hand. Today's unemployment statistics show that among the youth in this country there are some 21.4 per cent unemployed. One in every five young people in this country is without a job. Not only are the heads of families, those who have to pay the mortgage, and pay for the groceries, suffering from the present state of our economy and the reluctance of Government to come to grips with the whole question of technological change, but the young people, who are the very future of this country, are suffering in a very deep way from the present economic crisis which exists in Canada.
A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) presented to the House his plan with regard to technological change. He spoke about incentives to the private sector. He spoke about a rosy future for Canada. He spoke about the prospects of Canadians moving from boring, tedious, difficult jobs into exciting and well paid jobs. While this can be part of the picture with regard to technological change, it is not the whole picture. We all become very vividly aware of the fact that the Minister had only presented one side of the picture the next morning when The Globe and Mail published a secret document with regard to technological change which the Minister had in his possession. It was a document which pointed out some of the challenges which are involved in the transition from our present economy to the new economy.
One of the stark realities which is involved in this transition is the fact of the possible loss of some two million jobs for the Canadian economy, and the fact that unless something serious is done about the situation we could be facing unemployment rates in this country of some 15 per cent by the year 1990. Therefore, while the budget which the Government recently introduced in the House accepted unemployment at 12 per cent for this year, 11 per cent for next year and 10 per cent for subsequent years, and in fact suggested that full employment in this country was going to mean unemployment at some 7 per cent or 8 per cent in the long term, this secret document, which the Government has yet failed to release, shows that we may face unemployment rates of up to 15 per cent if the Government does not take seriously the whole question of technological change.
The problem with the approach which the Government is taking to technological change and to the over-all economy is
Supply
that it has really decided to wash its hands of the responsibility of leadership in the economic area. It has decided to rely on the private sector. The budget document indicates over and over again that the jobs will have to come from the private sector. The problem with that is, Mr. Speaker, that if you leave the creation of jobs and growth of the economy to the private sector, and the private sector only, then you are leaving our future and the important decisions with regard to our future to the individual heads of individual business enterprises in this country.
This is a time when we need more than ever an over-all strategy for the direction of the economy of this country and a time when we need our public institutions to bring together business, investment communities, labour and the public sector in a common effort to devise a strategy for economic development, and a strategy for economic development which will have as its first priority the provisions of employment for all Canadians. Rather than putting in place an industrial strategy, a plan of economic development in this country, what the Government has done in its most recent budget, is to rely on incentives to the private sector. It took whatever financial elbow room it had and allocated those dollars to the private sector. At the same time it failed to set a direction for the Canadian economy. That is the first major failing of this Government in its efforts to deal with technological change.
Another thing I want to bring to the attention of this House, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that obviously when we move into a very different kind of economy, when technological change is going to have a comprehensive impact upon the kind of work taking place in the country, when even established industries are going to renew themselves and take a different form, it is crucial that we have an adequate training system. In other words, there is going to be so much change going on in the economy that in order for people to have work and adequate and secure incomes, they will need to have ready and easy access to adequate training. Yet what is the Government's record in this area? When it brought in the National Training Act, which has been touted and advertised across this country, it continued with the same old approach to training which had been in place for a number of years now. That consists of giving financial incentives to the private sector to train people. But that does not really put in place a training system such as exists in European countries, for example. What I am referring to is the fact that in this country our industry trains fewer of its workers than do comparable industries in European countries.
That is why when the debate was going on in the House with regard to training we suggested that the Government examine seriously the grant levy system of training. The notion behind this system is that we would take a particular part of the manufacturing industry, let us say, and we would levy a company in that industry a certain amount to be put in the pot for training. Then those companies which actually did the training could take something out of the pot. That system
25234

May 6, 1983
Supply
would encourage industry to train people. It is using both the carrot and the stick. If Canadians are to have access to jobs with higher skill levels, it is crucial that private industry be brought into the training business and that it be systematized, and not just rely upon cash grants and cash incentives.
Another area where the impact of technological change is very striking is that of the disadvantaged people, whether it be women, natives or the handicapped. I would like to focus on women for a moment because they make up a large part of service sector employees. That sector will be radically changed by new technology. The jobs women presently occupy, in which they are underpaid relative to men, are going to be deskilled or lost. So that if women are not to bear the burden of this transition from the old technology to the new, programs have to be put in place to guarantee that adequate training is made available to women to allow them to take advantage of newly created jobs so they can continue to earn an adequate living. Not only will there need to be training put in place, but adequate social support will be needed so that women with children can take the available training.
In this country, Mr. Speaker, there is a very large percentage of people who are functionally illiterate. At a time when we are moving into an era of new technology, it is fairly obvious that those people will be left behind and will continue to be forgotten by the economy unless we do something serious in this area. The Government has yet to put into place a serious and comprehensive program to deal with the existence of functional illiteracy in this country. Clearly, if they are going to have a chance to earn a living in this society which demands very high skill levels, they need to have the basic skills to allow them to take the training necessary for new jobs.
Some people pin their hopes for jobs on support of the high technology strategy. But we know from the comments of people such as the Canada Council on Social Development, which has analysed this situation, that while high technology will provide some employment it will not provide sufficient employment for all Canadians. It is going to be necessary to have in place a permanent and comprehensive kind of direct job creation system. The present system is ad hoc and temporary, where the names of programs change from month-to-month or year-to-year, and where there are numerous announcements about job creation but there is no permanent and comprehensive plan to provide employment for all those who cannot find it in the private sector.
Fundamentally, technological change offers us a challenge. It challenges the basic value, of our society as a whole and us as individual citizens. When the Minister spoke the other day he gave a very rosy picture of technological change and seemed to give us a kind of candy store approach to technological change. He had us going into the candy store as if we were children, picking a bonbon here, a licorice there, and generally enjoying ourselves. But that was not the full picture of the impact of technological change on our society.
The Conservatives have focused exclusively on research and development and investment in R and D. That reminds me a bit of the old economist who used to think that gold was the
source of wealth and riches. Well, that sort of economic theory is passe these days because we know that the real source of wealth and riches in this society is its people. Our fundamental commitment to people and the notion that everyone has the right to a job is the source of real value in society. We have to decide now whether technological change will be a burden on the backs of people or whether it will serve people. If it is going to serve people, then we will have to find ways of redefining work, expanding our definition of work, and paying the newly developed jobs adequate salaries.
The change going on in society today is a radical change, Mr. Speaker. Traditionally, farming, for example, was done by hand with the help of a horse and plow. But when mechanization came to the farm, the whole nature of farming changed and the number of people needed was greatly reduced. It is this kind of drastic change which is taking place in our society and we need a plan to deal with it, to make the change serve Canadians rather than Canadians serve the change and suffer through very high levels of unemployment as the price of bringing new technology to Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the comments of my two friends on the opposite benches representing views from Newfoundland, on the one hand, and from a Manitoba perspective on the other. I am pleased, at least, that we do not seem to have any neo-Luddite type of talk coming from the Opposition. There seems to be a recognition that Canada must embark upon and embrace, if you like, the new technologies, which is what our technology policy is intended to do and, I believe, will do.
I do think that there is a certain amount of wallowing in gloom and doom and much concern expressed about a matter which is of concern to all of us. That is the issue, of course, of unemployment. However, we must never lose sight of the fact that today's unemployment results from a combination of factors, one of which is clearly the recession through which the whole western industrialized society is currently moving-and moving out of, I might say. That is something about which one can be optimistic. However, we cannot neglect the fact, of course, that there is high unemployment in all countries. High unemployment and recession in countries where we send our goods will have a major impact on the Canadian economy for as long as the situation lasts. We know that. I believe that Canadians, through this recession, have come to realize the extent to which Canada is very much a part of the world trading community.
That being said, I frankly do not intend to engage in a lot of political rhetoric. I really feel that this debate deserves careful and thoughtful presentation by all who wish to engage in it. Some of the issues that we are considering are really issues for the future. They are issues of the Canada of tomorrow. I intend to deal with them in that light. It is a very important
May 6, 1983

discussion and one which I frankly welcome. It should be thoughtful and not hysterical. People should not be spooked by these opportunities which the new technologies are bringing to us and to other societies. The challenges must be addressed in a rational way, and I suggest that that is what we have been doing and what we will continue to do.
Therefore, I implore Hon. Members: do not cloud the issues. Let us clarify the issues. Let us have a dialogue which may begin in the House and stretch the full breath of the land so that Canadians will be more aware of what lies ahead, the challenges and the opportunities. I think I can satisfy Hon. Members in the House today in the course of these remarks that the opportunities are there, that all the scenarios possible are optimistic scenarios, the only exception being the neoLuddite school, in other words, the standstill philosophy which, of course, Canadians would not accept and which could only bring with it lower standards of living and certainly devalued currency, and would truly move us into the backwater of the progress sweeping the rest of the world. That Canadians will not accept.

First, Mr. Speaker, I realize that a document drafted in my Department has prompted this debate. It is an internal and confidential document which, apparently, was given to a Globe and Mail journalist. The document cannot really be described as a study and it cannot even be said to be a report. It was to be the basis of a debate with my colleagues and the starting point of discussions on the major issues with which the Canadian economy will have to come to grips over the next ten years. It is more properly a working paper which Ministers might consult when reviewing economic development priorities at the national and even the regional levels.
In the discharge of my duties as Minister of State for Economic Development, Mr. Speaker, I think it is my responsibility, and I should always bring to the attention of my colleagues and the Canadian public the challenges we must face thanks to that technological revolution. Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity today to clarify the situation rather than paint it black.

That being said, let me review briefly the notice of motion proposed by the Opposition. It could really be divided into three parts. The first part deals with the issue of funding. It purports to condemn the Government or seeks the condemnation by the House of the Government for its failure to provide adequate and purposeful funding for research and development and specialized training necessary to cope with technological change in the workplace. This question has been debated and commented upon at some length since the budget was brought down. In fact, as we know, the budget provided over $700 million of incremental, direct, federal-and I underline "federal"-funding in this area. In addition, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) tabled with the budget a discussion
Supply
paper on the issue of research and development. He wants to know, and we want to know, what are the best techniques?
As studies show, we have one of the richest fiscal incentive regimes in all of the industrialized world, that is, with regard to stimulation of research and development in the private sector. However, perhaps it needs some fine-tuning. Perhaps it needs some enrichment here or there. That is what this open public discussion on the basis of the document tabled yesterday should show.
I would point out that, in terms of the commitment to increased research and development in all sectors, we are doing very well. Let us not consider it from a point of view of gloom and doom or-
[ Translation]
As I said a moment ago, by painting the situation in black, because frankly I can see that our policy will have a very promising outcome.

I see, for example, that we are on track with rising to 1.5 per cent of spending as a percentage of Gross National Product by 1985. That is something which is to be applauded. I think that the effort made by the private sector, by industry and by all communities in recent years has been very encouraging indeed. Of course, the motion speaks of specialized training.

I would like to refer to the speech which was delivered by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), when he tabled his budget. Here is an excerpt:
To take full advantage of technological advances, Canada will increasingly need well-educated and well-trained workers. Moreover, workers will have to acquire new skills and knowledge throughout their working lives. With this in mind, I am allocating tonight an additional $155 million for human resource development programs. This will bring to $1.2 billion this year the funds allocated for skills development in occupations that are significant for economic growth. Over 250,000 Canadians, half of them young people, will benefit this year from federal support for human resource development.

What else needs to be said? We heard durirg Question Period today, as well, the response of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) when he outlined the vast array of programs and the amount which is being spent on human resource development. Therefore, I really do not think that the Hon. Member's notice of motion is in fact well founded when it comes to the commitment of the Government in terms of expenditures themselves.
Let me consider the second part of the motion which was put forward. We speak of a displacement of jobs in manufacturing and in business services. Reference is made to the so-called Government study. As I said in my opening comments, there really is no Government study. There was a discussion document which was there to promote discussion, and it obviously has had that effect, partly through the leak of which we are all aware.

May 6, 1983
Supply
As the Hon. Member knows, there is much debate in the western world at the present time about what the impact of these new technologies may be. I was looking at the comments of the well known economist, Michael McCracken, which he aparently made during a radio interview in the course of this week. He takes very serious issue with the idea of job loss. He said perhaps the contrary, that if we do not embark on these new technologies, the result will be a much greater job loss, and I think we would all agree with that. He does not necessarily accept the view that these new technologies will bring about job loss.
What do we mean by job loss? I must say that I become somewhat alarmed when I see headlines such as "Job Loss Study". There is a very big difference between unemployment and job loss. If we automate and introduce robotics, if we introduce new systems for flexible manufacturing and provide more automation, surely there will be a job loss in that sector. It has long been predicted in all the industrialized countries that there would be a job loss in the manufacturing sector. I will come to the question of whether that is a bad occurrence in a few moments when I review some authorities on the subject. I do not believe that it is bad, and I suggest that I am supported by most independent studies. There will be a job loss, but what about the job gains? How many jobs will be created? What new opportunities will arise from these new technologies? Those are the questions that we must address. Does anyone really know the answer?
In that regard I would suggest that economists are very divided on this issue. There is an old saying about economists that if all the economists in the world were laid end to end, they would still point in all directions. Nothing could be more true when it comes to this debate. That is not to criticize economists, because they too have stimulated debate and put forward ideas. The fact is that I do not believe anyone completely understands these issues because no one has a crystal ball that can tell us what new opportunities will arise, just as we did not know what the automobile would do in terms of shopping centres, tourism, trailer homes and all those things that have evolved from the new transportation system. How do we know what the new information society will bring?
There is much reason to believe that it will bring a lot of good jobs. In fairness, let me say that there are two schools of thought on the subject. I would like to refer to both of them. One school of thought says that there will be more better paying jobs. That is an optimistic scenario and one that is obviously founded upon the historical pattern of technology and technological change. This is a serious school of thought and one that already has a certain amount of evidence to support its thesis.
For example, I refer to an article by Richard Riche who is a senior supervisory economist employed by the U.S. Department of Labour. This article comes from "Economic Impact" No. ^l, 1983. He says this:
When computers were first introduced for office data applications, predictions were made that large numbers of clerical and kindred workers would be
displaced; and job opportunities for millions of people, in what is one of the largest occupational employment categories, would be curtailed.
What actually did happen in the United States was quite different. In 1960 clerical workers numbered about 10 million and accounted for about 15 per cent of total U. S. employment. By 1980 there were more than 18 million clerical workers and they accounted for about 19 per cent of the total. Thus, instead of clerical worker employment decreasing as had been predicted, employment increased about 85 percent between 1960 and 1980. And clerical employment is projected to continue to increase significantly to 1990.
That regards the clerical sector about which much concern has been expressed.
Of course, the other sector is the manufacturing sector and the impact of robots there. With respect to robots, there are also some interesting comments in this same report. I read from page 23 where it states:
One survey of users and manufacturers of robots suggests that about 95 per cent of the jobs displaced by robots between now and 1990 will not involve unemployment because workers will be either retrained or, in some cases, retire because of age.
I can deal with the programs that are necessary for that, but we should not lose sight of it. There is much more, but I fear that time does not permit me to read all this into the record. I would be very happy to make some of this available to my hon. friends because I am sure they would find it interesting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that because I enjoy the calibre of the debate, and I believe it is an important one as it may be the beginning of a debate that will take place across the country. We will be able to address some of these issues which are very important, particularly to the generation of young Canadians who are so concerned about their future. I think it is important for us to realize what the opportunities and challenges are.
Let me continue this interesting comment on robots. It says:
Although it would seem logical that the initial impact of the installation of robots would be to reduce employment and, sometimes, to create some unemployment, this has not actually been the case to any great extent. The purpose of the introduction of robots is to improve productivity, thereby enhancing the competitiveness of the firm and the welfare of individuals associated with it. The existence and size of the initial employment effects are often overstated, since the reduction in work force resulting from the introduction of robots is partly offset by the hiring of maintenance personnel, workers to manufacture robots, and computer programmers to provide instructions.
It should be noted that the structure of employment will change in what most persons would regard as a positive direction.
I emphasize this:
Robots will usually replace workers engaged in monotonous tasks that are often physically overly demanding and mentally unrewarding. Sometimes, too,
May 6, 1983

the jobs taken over by robots are dangerous for humans. In these cases, the displaced workers may ultimately welcome robots as a means of freeing them to do more rewarding tasks.
I think that is a significant point that must be made in the context of this discussion.
We have another school of thought which tells us that we may indeed have more wealth through the new technologies but less jobs. That school also has some very credible spokesmen. One of the most credible is Wassily Leontief who was a Nobel prize winner in 1973. Leontieffs article, which I read and found interesting, can be found in Scientific American of September, 1982. This Scientific American publication is entirely devoted to issues on the mechanization of work. Leontief postulates that there indeed may be permanent job loss through these new technologies, and he bases himself in part on the only model he could find, which was Austria.
Some years ago Austria did a study of the effects of new technologies on the Austrian economy. He says:
The projections that carry the present state-of-the-art laborsaving technology into full application everywhere in the Austrian economy by 1990 lead in all cases to the largest increase in gross domestic product-
That is to say the most wealth:
-but also to the highest levels of unemployment, to unemployment of 10 percent, a level not experienced in Austria since the dark days of the 1930s. With curtailment in the length of the work week at the maximum degree of mechanization, the direction of both the positive and the negative changes remains the same but their absolute magnitudes are reduced. Unemployment in this case comes closer to the civilized Austrian experience of 2 percent.
Of course, he makes the argument that if that scenario is correct, we will have to address some major changes that will have to take place in the nature of work.
I remind the House that the work week has dropped from 67 hours 100 years ago down to 40 hours today. I do not believe that we should say that this is a dismal scenario that we are seeing. I suggest to my hon. friends that no matter which of these two positions is correct, either more better paying jobs or indeed less jobs through mechanization, but more wealth in both cases, we have the means at our disposal to address the problems because society will be the richer for it.
The only scenario where that does not take place is if we back away from our commitment to technology and the technological revolution. If we back away from it then, of course, we will see a fall in our standard of living. We will see a devalued currency. We will see massive unemployment because we simply will not be competitive in the international marketplaces and, I suppose, we will become the traditional hewers of wood and drawers of water.
There is tremendous excitement ahead for us. There are great opportunities. I would say that one could take either of the scenarios. I prefer the optimistic scenario because we have been that way in the past. We have been down that road. We have seen it happen in agriculture. Between 1946 and 1961 we lost half a million jobs in agriculture. We have seen employment in agriculture between 1946 to 1981 drop from 25 per cent of the work force to 4 per cent of the work force. I do not think anybody would consider those jobs lost; those are jobs displaced. But again of those scenarios-and I will just close

my comments with this one point-whether we have more better paying jobs or whether we have less jobs but more wealth in both cases, in either of them we have a transitional period that we have to address.
