subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today is not only timely but it is crucial to
Supply
the future development of Canada. We can either move with confidence into the twenty-first century or we can linger behind as suppliers of raw material to the other industrialized nations of the world. That choice is ours.
We are overwhelmed almost daily by new technological advances. As Alvin Toffler puts it, we are encountering the third wave and Canada cannot afford to ride that wave on imported technology, nor can we afford to use our limited cash resources to develop products that no one can sell.
Speaking for the riding of St. Catharines, I am naturally interested in research and development and the advantages that a vigorous R and D program might have for the shipbuilding and automotive industries. Both of those industries have been harder hit during this recession than most other segments of our society.
A moment ago, I heard the Minister speak rather disparagingly of the Opposition as purveyors of doom and gloom. Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that it is not our purpose and intent to make known the facts simply on the basis of preaching doom and gloom, but we want the country to know that things could be different if the process were different and if the programs were different. We are here simply to set out the facts and the records of the Government as they are.
We have heard some reference made to Japan in the course of the debate. I would like to make more such references. I will not dwell too long on the fact that the Japanese automobile and shipbuilding industries have competed vigorously and successfully here in Canada and throughout the world. Indeed, in terms of the automobile, the Japanese now control between 25 and 35 per cent of the Canadian market. This success has come about in large part because their Government, management and labour have been able to pool their resources and talents, their knowledge and experience toward the development and production of marketable goods.
Shipbuilding is perhaps the best example of the co-operative, pragmatic approach of the Japanese. As technology advanced and the capital equipment of the Japanese shipyards became obsolete and as the decision was made by the Japanese Government to exploit the world market, the Japanese essentially closed their shipyards for a period of some two years. They closed to regroup, retool and retrain. After that hiatus, the Japanese stormed the world and are now in control of over 50 per cent of the shipbuilding market.
There are several lessons that could be learned from this example, not the least of which is that Government and industry-sponsored research signals the need and the value of putting industry in Canada today on an entirely new footing. Research gave the Japanese an edge, the edge needed to give them a competitive advantage. On the automotive side, the Japanese were not only able to anticipate the rising demand for smaller cars and trucks, they were able to continue upgrading their production through style, design, construction and engineering methods to put those vehicles on world markets. It comes as no surprise that the Japanese are investing heavily in

May 6, 1983
Supply
research and development. At present that investment amounts to 2.4 per cent of their GNP.
By comparison, the Canadian Government has left our shipbuilding and automotive industries to get along as best they can on the research and development side. Even worse, the Government has actively assisted exporting countries in both these two industries to gain stronger footholds in the Canadian market. Industries locked into price and marketing wars with imports find it more and more difficult to free up the research and development dollars needed by themselves. As those dollars diminish, the industries' ability to stay ahead of changing technology and consumer trends also diminishes.
I recognize that to accuse a Government of working against the interests of industries such as the automotive and shipbuilding industries is a serious charge. Yet there is no other conclusion one could reach when one considers the Government's action with respect to each of those industries. The shipbuilding industry was promised a shipbuilding policy as early as the spring of 1980. Three years went by before any action was taken. During that time even Petro-Canada was out buying offshore. To the credit of the Canadian shipbuilding industry, lay-offs were delayed and minimized to an extent that belied the extreme difficulties they were experiencing. While Petro-Canada was buying offshore, the Government was busy taxing away what business the industry could generate. All Hon. Members will recall the discriminatory tax imposed on marine bunker fuel. A number of Government Members spoke out strongly against that tax, and then went on to vote for it when it was before the House. The industry mounted a strong lobby to oppose the tax, but to little or no avail.
Running concurrently with that furore was the November budget proposal-and now the law-to halve the capital cost allowance for the first year of acquisition. This measure added hundreds of thousands of dollars to the tax liability of a prospective ship owner. Orders fell off, to no one's surprise.
One can be forgiven for thinking that these two measures were the only ones with which the industry had to cope. They are bad enough, but we cannot forget the hike in seaway tolls and lockage fees which contributed to the decline in shipping. Transportation is a highly competitive industry where a cent per tonne difference in price decides whether a customer will use the transportation mode of a railway, shipyard or truck, inside or outside Canada.
The Americans encountered similar economic difficulties. They took action to put their railways on a more competitive footing, an action opposite to the direction being taken by the Canadian Government with respect to shipping. Hence, while shipping costs were going up because of Government-imposed taxes and fees, United States rail costs were going down because Americans entered into a deregulation exercise. I point out these factors and considerations to demonstrate that the industries in question can only allocate money for research and development if they have money remaining after paying their operational expenses. For the Government to nail the
private sector for not spending enough while taxing the sector beyond reason is simply hypocritical.
Despite the albatross of high taxation and discriminatory policies, the private sector has managed to undertake some impressive research and development programs. Some of the programs have led to growth and prosperity for some sectors, while others have been able to maintain their viability by new product innovations. However, far too many businesses and industries have not been able to stay ahead of research and development in their fields, while others have come to rely upon imported technology. If we believe it is important that Canadian research and development be homegrown to the greatest possible extent-and I do-the federal Government will have to assist industry and its promotion and development more than it is presently doing.
After 15 years of neglect the Government is now proposing that a goal of 1.5 per cent of GNP be reached as quickly as possible for the support of research and development. That is almost a full percentage point behind that of the United States, Japan and West Germany. By way of contrast, the 1979 Progressive Conservative Government established a goal of 2.5 per cent. Our view was and is that Canada has lost ground which it has to make up. It not only lost ground before 1979 but has lost even more since then.
It is simply inadequate to throw money at a problem. There is no end to the projects which might be funded by someone somewhere. This can always be used as a plausible case for the value of funding a particular area of research. Tough decisions have to be made. In times of economic difficulties perhaps those decisions are even tougher, but we must face them and go with areas of endeavour which show the greatest promise.
In keeping with this Government's approach, I note that $1.5 million of the $100 million in new high technology spending will be allocated to public relations. The best public relations in the world are more jobs and greater economic prosperity, not the further expenditure of public dollars on Government advertising to perpetrate a myth. After all, when we compare the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars on advertising for Petro-Canada with the decreasing support for Petro-Canada by Canadians, we might conclude that Government advertising has a negative effect upon Canadians.
High technology is a booming sector of the economy. It is creating thousands of jobs where few existed before. It is not the net sum of employment. High-tech businesses are usually very profitable and are responsible corporate citizens. They are having little or no difficulty convincing a country with high unemployment that high-tech is one of the bright stars on the horizon. We might then wonder whether the Government's $1.5 million public relations program is not ultimately designed to associate it with a success story instead of an unparalleled record of failures.
I mentioned unemployment a moment ago. That crisis is the second aspect of the motion before us today. St. Catharines-Niagara has been extremely hard hit by unemployment,
May 6, 1983

primarily because of the Government's inept and incompetent handling of the economy. Wonderful promises were made in 1980 about an industrial strategy, lower interest rates and lower energy prices. These were to happen, but once the election of February 1980 was over the Government proceeded to lead Canada into the worst economic downturn since the Great Depression. The Niagara, as an industrialized region, felt this more than most. Over the last year the St. Catharines-Niagara reporting area has more often than not been among the worst three urban centres for unemployment in Canada. Last month, as Government Members were quick to point out, unemployment dropped by almost 2 per cent in the Niagara, putting us as fourth worst in Canada. What Government Members fail to mention, though, is the fact that better unemployment statistics are coming forward because people are removing themselves from the labour market. They are just giving up any hope of finding a job. In the Niagara some 10,000 to 20,000 people are in this category. If those persons become heartened by the Government's optimistic and selfcongratulatory mouthings and rejoin the labour force, the unemployment rate in the Niagara would be at at least the minimum which we projected of 22 per cent.
There is little comfort to be gained from lower unemployment statistics when the reason behind them is the despair and despondency of many thousands of Canadians. Even now, with all the benefits of the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), there were 7,000 fewer jobs in industrial Canada than in the month previous, and the unemployment rate in Ontario rose in the last month from 11.4 per cent to 11.7 per cent. The Niagara area fared even worse than that.
A significant number of those who are now unemployed can expect a brighter future when and if economic recovery takes hold, but many will not have that brighter future, Mr. Speaker, because they will not have the skills to accommodate and to meet the needs of that future. The motion before us draws attention to this fact and cites a federal study's conclusion that unemployment could reach 15 per cent by 1991. That is a figure we might have to live with. We cannot expect, nor should we, to raid other countries for the skilled workers needed to fill some select Canadian jobs, as we so often have done in the past. Surely, we can train our own people for our own jobs and prospects.
Study after study, including the parliamentary task force report "Work for Tomorrow", has cried out for more retraining programs to put Canadians in a position to fill those jobs requiring new or upgraded skills. The Government's response has been totally inadequate. It seems that the Government would rather issue Unemployment Insurance cheques than to use that money and the innate willingness of the unskilled worker to receive training to sponsor a national drive to get Canadians ready for the challenges which lie ahead.
The high-tech revolution can be a positive and welcome one for Canada if we are prepared to stay ahead of it. Nevertheless, if we continue to drift as we are now, that revolution will neither be as great nor as positive as it should be. The time for
Supply
action is fast running out, Mr. Speaker. Let us get on with the job now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some trepidation. This is a rather important debate. The tone was set this morning by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and reinforced by the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party and the Minister.
It is an interesting fact that most of us on both sides of the House do attach much importance to the subject of job creation and what I may call the "cybernetic revolution" we are facing. The fact is that we have a challenge to meet, but as Canadians, I am sure we have the energies and the potential will to do so with success. Rather than speak gloomily about the subject, I would like to address it on two aspects dealing with the revolution. First, I would like to speak to the research and development component of the motion. Second, I would like to address the question of training and development of our human resources which is our Canadian wealth in the future.
I would like to clarify for Hon. Members certain statements made about the level of research and development funding in Canada and about this Government's commitment to increasing R and D so that we do meet our investment target of 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1985. Canada has passed through a period of relatively low investments in research and development, but this trend has now been reversed. In 1982, Canada's gross expenditures and R and D reached 1.34 per cent of GNP, well on our way to meeting our target of 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1985. During the late sixties and for the first half of the seventies, there was a steady decline in the share of the GNP which was invested in R and D. As a percentage of GNP, Canada's gross domestic expenditures on R and D declined from what was then an all-time high of 1.29 per cent in 1969 to a low of 0.96 per cent in 1976. Spending by the Canadian business sector was particularly weak when compared to the expenditures of the industrial sectors of the major industrialized nations. Moreover, most of our international competitors were achieving larger productivity growths and our deficit in high technology trade was on the increase.
To provide Canadian industry with incentives to increase its R and D expenditures and by so doing increase its productivity and competitiveness in the domestic and international marketplaces, the federal Government introduced an R and D investment tax credit in 1977 and followed up in 1978 with an additional allowance for scientific research. Later, in December 1980, Cabinet endorsed an R and D Planning Framework which set a national target for R and D expenditures in the natural sciences and engineering to reach 1.5 per cent of GNP by 1985. Half of these investments were to be made by the industrial sector and one-third by the federal Government, with the remainder to be taken up by the other sectors. The

Supply
framework also established growth targets for gross domestic expenditures on R and D and for the expenditures of the various funding sectors. Beginning in 1979, gross domestic expenditures on R and D were to increase annually at an average rate of 20 per cent, with industrial support increasing at 27 per cent and federal funding to be fixed at 17 per cent.
Considerable progress has been achieved since the introduction of the tax measures and the adoption of the R and D plan. Over the period 1979-82, gross domestic expenditures on R and D have increased at an average rate of 20 per cent, industry's investment has grown at 26 per cent per annum, and the federal contribution has advanced yearly at a rate of approximately 18 per cent. These growth rates are almost identical to those contained in the R and D Planning Framework. The downward trend in the gross domestic expenditures on R and D to the Gross National Product ratio has been arrested and reversed. From 1976 onwards gross domestic expenditures have consistently increased at a faster rate than the GNP and, since the approval of the R and D Planning Framework, gross domestic expenditures on R and D, as a share of GNP, has increased from its base value of 1.03 per cent in 1979 to 1.34 per cent in 1982. In 1982, R and D expenditures in the natural sciences amounted to $4.7 billion, $833 million, or almost 22 per cent more than in the previous year. This is the largest year-over-year percentage increase ever recorded. During the same period federal funding of GERD increased by $232 million from $1.4 billion in the previous year to $1.6 billion in 1982. In real term, national R and D expenditures have increased each year since 1976 at an average of 7 per cent annually and between 1980 and 1982 have grown at 10 per cent per annum.
In addition to the support provided by grants, contracts and contributions, the federal Government also encourages industrial R and D through a variety of indirect measures. In 1980, for example, 343 firms filed claims amounting to $181 million in additional allowances for scientific research and $83 million in R and D investment tax credits. Corporate taxes were probably reduced by between $90 to $120 million as a result of these claims.
Federal assistance is also provided for other stages of the innovation process. In 1982, the major industry support programs spent $429 million to improve the innovative capabilities of Canadian industry.
More than half the $2.6 billion in industrial R and D was performed in high technology sectors such as communications equipment, aerospace, petroleum products and chemicals. These four sectors carried out $1,228 million of R and D in 1982, $255 million more than in the previous year and roughly twice the amount performed in 1979.
Preliminary data for 1983 suggested a slowing down in the growth of funding in both the federal Government and industry sectors. However, in the case of the federal Government, these data were based on the 1983-84 Main Estimates and did
May 6, 1983
not contain the expenditures from a number of Cabinet Committee decisions made since that time.
Nor did the data reflect the April 19 budget initiatives which include $100 million over the next two years for new technology policy initiatives, $180 million for high technology procurement and $290 million to be spent on new research facilities.
In the case of industry, the 1983 data are based on forecasts of expenditures derived from the 1982 industry survey. Once again, these forecasts do not anticipate the increased tax credit or flow through tax incentives proposed in the April 19 budget. These measures are expected to increase Government support of industry by some $185 million in the first full year in which they will apply and encourage substantial increases in industry funding. Even without these new incentives, other evidence suggests that the 1983 figures are conservative. For example, The Financial Post survey of industry R and D indicates 54 of 82 firms will increase their R and D expenditures in real terms over the next three years.
Of the $3,242 million allocated for science and technology expenditures in 1983-84, $2,611 million or 80 per cent will be for activities in the natural sciences and engineering. R and D in the natural sciences will amount to $1,956 million, 11 per cent more than last year, and in the related scientific activities expenditures will increase 12 per cent from $585 million to $655 million. Since 1979-80, expenditures on R and D and related scientific activities will have grown at annual rates of 15 per cent and 14 per cent respectively.
Approximately 52 per cent of the federal 1983-84 R and D program is allocated for projects relating to natural resources, including food and oceans, energy and the advancement of science. Another 11 per cent will be spent in response to initiatives from the industrial sector and 8 per cent on health R and D. In recent years, energy and space have been the fastest growing program areas with increases averaging 23 per cent per annum between 1981-82 and 1983-84.
Federal R and D expenditures in the industry sector will amount to $462 million, 27 per cent more than the 1982-83 level and more than twice the 1979-80 total of $213 million. Over the five-year period, federal funding of industrial R and D will have increased by 21 per cent per annum. Federal R and D expenditures on university R and D have grown by 17 per cent per annum during this period and by 15 per cent for federal intramural R and D.
During the 1983-84 fiscal year this Government will spend an estimated $631 on activities in the human sciences. This is 8 per cent more than the $583 million spent in 1982-83 and 59 per cent more than the 1979-80 expenditures of $397 million.
For all these reasons, this Government is confident that Canada will continue its progress toward the 1985 target of 1.5 per cent. I thank Hon. Members for letting me put these figures on the record because I do think they are important. As Members know, the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, which regularly goes through these exercises of
May 6, 1983

rather dry figures, is always interested, and I thought it would be appropriate at this time to make these public.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to speak to a matter that is closer to my riding and to your own riding of Ottawa West as well, namely, training and development.
As we all know, a number of companies in the Ottawa area are specialized in high technology I am thinking, for instance, of Mitel, which has made a tremendous contribution to Canada's economy by taking advantage of the latest modern technologies. I am of course delighted to see these companies expand, and in fact, Mitel recently announced it had obtained a very important contract for exporting telephone communications equipment.
Mr. Speaker, before going into the details of my subject, which is training and development, I would also like to draw the attention of the House today to an article in the Financial Post published under the title "High-tech booster", which revealed that "Canada's high-tech sector is well pleased by Finance Minister Marc Lalonde's April budget, which contains several significant investment changes and more than $500 million-worth of incentives".
Mr. Speaker, that appeared today, in the Financial Post.
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to read the whole article, although there are some very interesting explanations concerning the measures contained in the last budget which, as I said earlier, are likely to promote what is known as research and development, that is, things that are essential to the growth of our economy.
Organizations that reacted favourably to measures aimed at assisting progress in the technology sector also included the Canadian Advanced Technology Association, whose Executive Director, Mr. Robert Long, indicated that the result would be increased investment in this sector.
In an economy that is primarily based on private enterprise, I see these reactions as signs of a trend that will lead to practical projects and thus jobs, and that is worth a lot more than gratuitous statements to the effect the Government has failed to act in this area.
This is not to say that the situation is satisfactory or that we can look forward to a rosy future, because the unemployment rate remains high, despite our present economic recovery. It is clear that many workers who have been laid off in certain industries and certain sectors will never get back the jobs they had before. They will have to be redirected elsewhere, if possible to jobs where they can use the same skills, but in many cases, these workers will have to be retrained. In fact, the National Training Act, which was passed in the House last year, will enable the Government of Canada to spend nearly $1 billion on training and development. Mr. Speaker, I think these expenditures are essential, because they will help yound people to acquire the training they need to get jobs that require new skills.
Supply
We must look ahead and we cannot afford to listen to people who want to perpetuate industries that are labour-intensive but are technically obsolete in some areas and where foreign competition is practically eliminating us from the market. On the contrary, we must develop advanced technologies and not only maintain or improve our position on the domestic market but also make gains on market abroad. All this will also require the co-operation of provincial authorities-again, in connection with the National Training Act-because we all know that the provinces, which have jurisdiction in education matters, have a very substantial say in the development of occupational training programs.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read a comments from a talk by Dr. Larkin Kerwin, President of the National Research Council, who spoke to the Richelieu Club of Ottawa. This is in connection with what I just said about the problems of coordinating training programs to allow for both national priorities and the priorities of the provinces which are constitutionally responsible for education. I shall now quote Dr. Kerwin:
Unfortunately, there is no mechanism or co-ordinating body between the Federal Government and the provinces as far as scientific research and development is concerned, and as a result, it is difficult to define priorities in this respect. The sensible thing to do would be for both levels of government to agree on a common strategy, with definite emphasis on establishing high-technology industries.
We must therefore provide a comprehensive solution to this problem. We must urge the provinces, the universities and the entire post-secondary sector to work together with the Federal Government and sit down and determine our objectives, once and for all. That is why this morning, in the House, I asked the Minister whether he could count on the co-operation of the provinces. He answered, as Hon. Members will recall, that he had not yet approached the provinces. I hope, and I say this very sincerely, that all the provinces will sit down with the Federal Government in order to establish these mechanisms which are essential if we are to meet our common objectives, namely, training our human potential, our young people, in both technological and industrial skills.
It is no use going on about what happened in the past when workers were often trained for occupations where not enough jobs were available. From now on, we shall have to be very careful in selecting the kind of training we want to provide, not only as a matter of economics but also in order to maximize effectiveness.
In fact, the new program set up by the Department of Employment and Immigration contains a number of elements that will be very helpful in this respect.
First of all, we have the Canadian Occupational Projections System which makes it possible to collect, compile and transmit information on future manpower supply and demand, by

May 6, 1983
Supply
occupation. The program will help improve long-term human resources planning in Canada. There is also the Skills Growth Fund, which this year will make some $100 million available to Canadian institutions that are anxious to modernize or expand.
I am not unfamiliar with this fund, Mr. Speaker, because on March 17, here in the House, I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) for details about a grant provided by the fund to help create a training center for the high-technology industry here in Ottawa. The seven firms participating in this enterprise are: NABU, Epitek, Digital Equipment, Canadian Marconi, Mitel, Gandalf and System-house, which are now developing plans for this special training program. The participation of this consortium is a perfect example of co-operation between the Federal Government and the private sector in the context of training Canadians so they will be able to meet the challenges of the eighties.
Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning of my speech, to achieve high levels of employment and an increase in real wages, we must be able to provide Canadian workers with skills that are sought after by growth-sector industries. The key element of a labour market strategy for the eighties is therefore to improve and fine tune occupational training. The National Occupational Training Program, established under the National Training Act, has provided the basis for such action.
I see that you are rising, Mr. Speaker. If my time has expired, I am sorry, but I would have liked to continue my speech.

speechtext:
Thank you for giving me more time, Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. As I said earlier, our aim was to make sure that employers could find workers with the skills required to expand their businesses and to help individuals acquire the necessary skills to become more productive and more competitive on the labour market. The National Training Act determines where training funds will be allocated, that is mostly for training activities in occupations of national importance.
Mr. Speaker, the key elements of the training strategy to be implemented under the Act in order meet our needs are as follows, I shall be very brief because I would like to cover this most important issue as completely as possible. First, more information must be obtained about the needs for various skills. To this end, governments, business and labour must, of course, work together under the Canadian Occupational Forecasting Program.
Some changes must also be made to training and development facilities to help them provide the required training. The
various establishments must adapt to the new conditions in order to provide the training courses deemed necessary. This adaptation is difficult, I am told, because the increase the number of trainees is now at a standstill. Because of this, special funds will have to be earmarked for the expansion of training facilities in areas where the need is greatest. Projects funded by the Skills Growth Fund established under the National Training Act are already giving results, as in the case of the seven Ottawa companies I mentioned earlier.
Elsewhere, the British Columbia Institute of Technology, for instance, is already providng a computer design and manufacturing program. The Winnipeg Computing Devices Corporation has developed computer training courses for underprivileged youths and the Holland College in Prince Edward Island has a marine techniques program.
The quantity and quality of industrial training must therefore be improved. Particularly, on the job training for jobs geared to the growth of Canada should be increased. The revised Industrial Training and Critical Trades Skills Training Programs are essential tools for making the necessary improvements.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I remember spending many years of my life in school, from 1960 to 1972, when the number of technical schools in Canada grew tremendously under a program introduced by Mr. Diefenbaker in 1957 to encourage the provinces to build technical schools in order to meet the challenge of the 70s. We took up a challenge in 1980; in 1990, we shall have to get together, develop new techniques and direct our programs toward youth training.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Are there any Hon. Members rising to ask questions or make comments on the speech of the Hon. Member? If not, the Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean):

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the motion before the House today, that this House condemns the Government for its failure to provide adequate and purposeful funding for research and development and specialized training, necessary to cope with technological change in the workplace. According to a federal Government study this will cause serious displacement of jobs in manufacturing and business services, resulting in continuing high unemployment, forecast to reach 15 per cent by 1991. I do so because it is surely one of the most urgent issue before the nation. This issue is not just an international one but also one which confronts each of our constituencies.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), in introducing the motion today indicated that the Government is finally coming to a new realization, in part because of a study which was leaked to the public. The Government is being besieged by groups and sectors across the
May 6, 1983

society to give some leadership, in terms of a national effort, to deal with the changing times.
Now we are told that the Government is beginning a process of conditioning Canadians to a situation which might well have been avoided had there been, during the last 15 years, any reading of the signs of the times which are before us. As my colleague said, we are placed in a situation today where there are some 609,000 women and some 624,000 youth between the ages of 15 and 24 who are unemployed. They are the ones who are the first to go and the last back in the work force.
In his response in the debate, the Minister has set several scenarios before us and has sought to take attention away from the failure of the Government to plan through these years. He has suggested instead that we now play catch-up football. He tells that we are in a transitional period, of which we are all aware; and that this must be addressed, as it must be and on an emergency basis. There will now be a propaganda program in the schools called an awareness program and there will be a Canada Tomorrow Conference. Had the Minister and his officials been taking the warnings of the Science Council of Canada and those of other Government agencies seriously through the years, we would not be in this situation.
Speaking to the 1983 general meeting of faculty and staff at the University of Waterloo, an institution with world class technological capacity, the President, Dr. Douglas Wright, said:
The transformation of the economy now taking place, driven by new technologies and international competition, is leading to a more fundamental division in the labour force. In the next few years, unskilled workers will face rapidly declining prospects and the role of knowledge-based workers will become much more critical. Canada's future depends more on its human resources than on its natural resources. It seems no accident that the most successful economies in the world today are resource-poor and technology-rich. They all put a premium on rigour in education and training. They are all committed to maintaining longterm competitiveness through research and development.
By way of reflection on that comment I was interested to learn, for example, of the integration of universities and industry in Japan. At the University of Tokyo there are now some six professors of robotics in the engineering faculty. They feed their research and development directly into the Japanese car industry. Presently, 25 per cent of the cost of a car in Canada is in electronics and 90 per cent of that electronics comes from Japan into the North American automotive centres.
In an article in the Business Quarterly of 1982, Professor MacMillan suggests that before long even our base resources will not be needed. The Japanese are in the process of developing a ceramic base for engine blocks which will no longer require the traditional metals to be used.
Today we are at a point where there is need to help small businesses apply new technology. Small businesses persons in my area of southwestern Ontario in Kitchener-Waterloo say that they cannot often be accepted because they do not have a track record. The Government wants to continue on the safe route and they are left out.
Supply
I want to focus for a moment on 52 per cent of our society which has been rigorously studying the implications of new technology. That sector consists of women and the organizations that speak for them. I want to draw to the attention of the House and our nation the current participation by female workers in our economy, and then move on to some suggestions about the importance of retraining and training programs to ensure that women are not made to suffer the brunt of job displacement due to technological change in the work place.
Let us review for a moment labour participation. In 1982, there were some 4.844 million women in the paid labour force. That is over 50 per cent of all Canadian women. Of those women in the labour force, 65 per cent were under 45, and 45 per cent were women with children under the age of three. The overwhelming majority of these women were single, widowed, divorced or the sole support of dependants. In addition, almost half of the wives in two income earning families were married to spouses earning less than $15,000 a year.
In 1981, the average income of a women in the paid labour force was about $8,100, which is less than half the average male wage of $16,659. If only full time work is considered, the average woman today earns 58 per cent of her male counterpart's average wage. That is $12,069 compared to $20,719.
Let us consider the matter of retraining of women in high technology. From December, 1981, to December, 1982, the unemployment rate among women rose from 9 per cent to 12.1 per cent, an increase of 41 per cent. Seventy per cent of women in the paid labour force are concentrated in low paid job ghettos in the clerical, sales and service occupations. The situation there is not improving.
Between 1975 and 1980, the female share of good managerial, professional and technical jobs increased by 1.5 per cent while women's share of traditional female jobs increased by
3.5	per cent. The over-all number of women in the latter category is far more significant than the managerial category.
Women are also losing ground in teaching, traditionally one of the best occupations for them. Between 1975 and 1980, 66.7 per cent of new full time teaching jobs went to men.
To this dismal picture must be added the possible impact of high technology, the subject we are addressing today, on women in the paid labour force. The job ghettos in which the majority of women in the paid labour force are clustered are prime targets for the efficiency and productivity improvements made possible by the micro-chip revolution. Up to one million jobs presently performed by women may disappear by 1990.
While the total number of jobs may remain stable and even increase, depending on Canada's over-all success in developing this new industry, workers with existing skills, many of them women, may well find themselves displaced.
To further compound the problem, all indications are that the skills gap between the old jobs wiped out by the new technology and the new ones created may be too great to be bridged by on the job training alone. This is especially true of clerical work. In order to prevent massive unemployment among women and the attendant social consequences for them

May 6, 1983
Supply
and their families, and in order to prevent widespread opposition to the new technology, these displaced workers must be retrained.
My Party is not prepared to abandon one million female workers. It is committed to the following measures to ensure that the necessary retraining takes place. First, financial incentives, especially tax measures, for employers to retrain existing employees prior to the introduction of new technology which renders their present skills obsolete. Second, financial incentives to industry, educational institutions and the Provinces to enable them to provide training which is targeted not only at the new high-technology jobs but also, wherever possible, at the displaced workers. I notice that there is nothing like that in Bill C-150 which covers educational transfers. If the Government is going to put strings on these transfers, why not put some strings on the training for women? Third, the supplementing of on the job training by skill development leave or some other form of paid or subsidized educational leave.
Fourth, amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to permit recipients to take appropriate retraining programs without loss of benefits.
Fifth, amendments to the Canada Labour Code specify a minimum standard for employees under federal jurisdiction with respect to consultation prior to the introduction of technological changes into the workplace with respect to retraining and with respect to health and safety standards in relation to new technology. The Canada Labour Code amendments are particularly important to women since the vast majority are non-unionized and therefore cannot bargain for such protection.
We turn now to the matter of training for women. We note that at the same time as traditional women's jobs are disappearing women continue to enter the labour force in ever increasing numbers. Presently six out of ten new entrants are women, both recent graduates and older women, and this number is expected to increase to seven out of ten in the next decade. The majority of these women are still equipping themselves for traditional occupations. Second to teaching, clerical work is still the most common occupation for female Bachelor of Arts graduates. Most women with business diplomas become clerks, compared to the majority of their male counterparts with similar qualifications who go into sales or management.
Women coming out of educational institutions, or from the home, must be encouraged to move into non-traditional occupations, especially those areas expected to be "priority" occupations in the next decade, through such measures as specialized counselling and special training grants.
In particular, my Party is committed to the following measures in relation to training. First, the substantial expansion of the Outreach Programs which counsel women reentering the labour force while at the same time ensuring that these programs continue to be operated as much as possible by the client groups.
Second, significant expansion of the CEIC Program for nontraditional training for women to ensure that women obtain their fair share of Government-sponsored training places for non-traditional jobs-currently only 6.5 per cent of such spaces are occupied by women-and to provide fiscal incentives to employees to hire and to train women in non-traditional occupations.
Third, reorientation of Canada Employment Centres generally so that they no longer act as a barrier to women seeking to enter non-traditional jobs. It is interesting to note that studies continue to indicate that Canada Employment counsellors are still channelling women into clerical training programs.
I want to pay a special tribute to the women's groups in the Waterloo region who are making an important contribution to the study of the effects of high technological changes in the workplace in the midst of that area in the country which is beset by unemployment problems due to the slump in the automotive industry and other industries. The group community resources for women through this spokesperson, Wendy Newberry, says that in our Kitchener-Waterloo area alone hundreds of working women, many employed currently in the insurance industry, are already experiencing the effects of the transition to word processing equipment, from typewriters to electronically-based information systems from manual data processing. She said that she would be happy to ensure the Government receives the report of this group's findings as they become available this spring and that they are particularly eager to see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) act upon the recommendations of the Labour Canada report entitled "In the Chips: Opportunities, People, Partnerships," which was submitted to the Minister last Fall by his Department's task force on microelectronics and employment.
In the few moments that remain to me, I want to suggest that this sector, the sector of women, is but one of the sectors and this is but one illustration of the size of the problem in front of us. Already in this debate we have reversed some of the many possibilities that lie open to us. The Government had before it the detailed report of the Science Council of Canada. In that report, after looking at the effects and the economic imperatives of all of this technological change, the needs that we have been talking about for employment strategies, retraining programs, software skills, design systems, co-operative approaches between labour and management, the Council predicted a bleak future if Canada does not act quickly to maintain social and economic stability in the transition to an information society. That report states:
Many sectors of our manufacturing industry would be rendered obsolete, virtually overnight. Our trade balance, already precarious, might never recover. Structural unemployment could lead to permanent joblessness for many Canadians, a decline in living standards and, for some, emigration.
This future can be avoided if action is taken immediately. The Government has had warning, not just for a year but for years and, indeed, through the last decade. This debate is important. Even at this late date there is a requirement for all sectors to come together to agree upon those strategies, and we in presenting this motion do so in order that we can expose to
May 6, 1983

ourselves and to the Canadian public many of the opportunities and alternatives which we would lay before the Canadian public as we look forward to the opportunity of becoming the Government of Canada.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Are there any Hon. Members rising to ask questions? The Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you must remember I have probably the easiest riding in Canada to recall and I realized when you were hesitating that you were not going to look up my riding. Most people ask where it is!
Nevertheless, this subject is of great interest to me. The Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) referred to a book that I treat as a bible. It was written in March, 1982 and was put out by the Science Council of Canada entitled "Planning now for an Information Society". I am just pointing out the dangers here because in that book the Science Council shows where it anticipates being between 1985 and 1990 and the year 2000. The Science Council also refers to where we will be in the years 1980 to 1985. Things are happening so quickly. What the Science Council predicted for the years 1980 to 1985 has now occurred, and part of what was anticipated for 19851990 has occurred.
This fine report was produced a little over a year ago. I am not criticizing the report; I am just getting my point across. What I am concerned about is not unemployment as such because that is an over-simplification of the problem. We have a social problem, a serious social problem, because technology will affect every facet of life. Today it is not necessarily taking jobs away from the workers.
I happen to have General Motors close by and part of its operation is in my own riding. I have been through the plant and I have studied what is happening. General Motors has not really reduced the number of employees. The reason General Motors put in robotics and got into high technology was not to reduce employment or cut employment costs but to improve the product and quality. The quality control is far greater when you have automatic welders as compared to humans, with their frailties and weaknesses. It is these frailties and weaknesses that concern me about high technology, not only the unemployed.
I do not believe that because of the baby boom we are going to have the serious unemployment we anticipated, but we are going to have a great deal of time. I do not say leisure time because that is a dangerous term. When you refer back to the days of Rome, it was leisure time that destroyed their society. In any event, we will have time.
One of the things we can do with our time is construct new projects. That would be an interesting use of our time. High technology will provide us with that. It will also provide us with access to information throughout the world, the upgrading of medical information and medical science to keep us healthy. It will give us easier access to stores in order to make purchases. This will be particularly helpful to the handicapped
Supply
who are unable to leave their homes. We will have a great deal of extra time.
A number of times one of my colleagues from British Columbia has talked about farmers who, because of the economy, have had to get an extra job off the farm. They have had to do this in order to maintain their farm, which is their basic interest. The Department of National Revenue is now going through its books and beginning to tax these people on their basic income. That is negative input. We should be developing tax incentives for individuals. Our basic industry was that of being hewers of wood and drawers of water. Those people individually and collectively can develop new technology for growing trees and producing a higher volume of grains. Let us look at corn, for example. Formerly corn could only be grown in the southernmost part of Ontario. It can now be grown in Manitoba. Each farmer who has an enterpreneurial spririt wants to do something along that line. I maintain that what the Department of National Revenue has done to these people is wrong.
With the extra time that will be available, it is very important to develop new skills, products, hybrids, the cross-pollination of different cereal grains and grasses. Therefore, it is very important that we encourage the small farmer. More people will be going back to the land. Through high technology and because there simply will not be as much employment in the manufacturing centres, more people will move into mid-Canada and develop their own interest and industry within that area. We will get away from the megacities which we have created through our material needs. We have to look at what we can do for the farm people through individual efforts. Also, we must look at biotechnology. We are not addressing ourselves to that. It is a very important subject because it may improve the strain of anything that grows. With improved medical science, people will be able to do more with their extra time. It is important that that time be filled.
As I said in question period today, we cannot fill that time with pay television. That is a crutch. We must give people a tool. That is what high technology will do. It will give people access to information. They will have access to debates in this House of Commons going back 20 years. People will have access to information in magazines from around the world. There will be international communication of information. What is going to happen will be exciting, but we have to identify what people are going to do with their time. We cannot call it leisure time or it will have no purpose.
Someone said to me that he can imagine the time when he will work three days a week. He will be able to devote over 50 per cent of his time to what he is interested in and yet retain the same basic income to maintain his standard of living. If that can be spread across the country, imagine how much benefit this country will get from people developing new ideas, new concepts, new methods of harvesting and growing, new forms of energy that we have not yet touched in this country. We keep talking about drilling for oil. We go five miles underground. We go out into the oceans into iceberg alley to

May 6, 1983
Supply
try and find oil. I was told today that in Nova Scotia they can produce almost enough alcohol to replace the oil they bring in from overseas.

speechtext: They need that in Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
That type of technology has been developed by individuals in the United States in such places as Kentucky, where they run their tractors on gasohol. We do not have that incentive in this country. This is what we must do.
Giving grants to large corporations is not the answer. We must assist these individuals. Let me give an explanation of grants. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) stated that he is providing larger funding. It usually takes the bureaucrats about a year to decide whether something is a worthwhile subject to be studied. By the time the grant is made, it represents less than 10 per cent of the total cost because usually the project has been completed.
If you really want to help industry in research and development, and that is where you want to put your effort, you should allow these people to remove deferred income tax payable from their financial statement. This would put their statement in a much stronger position. The free enterprise market will then come up with the money. They can borrow debt capital without future income tax on their statement. The Government will not collect it anyway, so why not wipe it off their sheets and allow them to go to the free market to raise funds? That is what industry wants, not grants because they take too long.
I have talked to Walter Light of Northern Telecom many times. He is a Canadian for whom I have the highest respect. He has done one of the most amazing jobs in this country to represent us in the communications field. I do not say he did alone, but he was the leader. He does not need grants. We are talking S700 million over two years. On one project alone, Northern Telecom will be spending $1.2 billion over the next five years. I am bringing high technology up because that is how it should be financed.
Going full circle, it is the individuals we must talk about. It is the potential unemployment that many Members have referred to and, as the Hon. Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) said, the unemployment of women that we must talk about. Well, Mr. Speaker, this week I spoke to a young lady who happens to work in the United States. Where she works, they have placed terminals in people's homes so that those people who used to come to the office to type now type within their own home. The typing is processed within their own home and printed in the office. We are going to come to that. There is a new book on this subject called "Megatrends" that tells us that in the future we will be taken away from the centre of the city and, perhaps going almost too far, we will all work in our own homes and not go to an office. The only thing that is missing there is the social interchange and the opportunity to discuss things one on one.
I do want to stress that we must deal with the social impact of technology. We must protect the people. Let me talk about structural unemployment, a subject which many people have referred to. Structural unemployment really refers to those people who cannot accept this new technology, people who were raised in an age when they used their hands. We must protect those people. We must assist them to relocate, to retrain, to do whatever is possible to assist them. If that fails, we must assist them to live with dignity. That is something that we are not dealing with.
A person from the age group of 20 to 45 can adapt very quickly to new technology. Some people in their middle years and older have a hard time grasping the new technology. Those are the people that will be seriously hurt. I feel that the youth will be picked up in time because they can go to community colleges and they can gain the knowledge that is needed, but it is the people who cannot do this that we must protect. At this point, the Government has not identified what is to be done about this problem.
About two months ago I talked to two young men who worked for General Motors. I said: "I hope you realize that your children will probably not have the same jobs you have". They replied: "Why is that?" I said: "Have you noticed the new robots in your plant?" They said: "Yes, we think they are wonderful". I said: "Has it not reduced the number of employees required per car manufactured?" They said: "Yes, it has". So I said: "You probably come from a family in Oshawa who came from a generation of people who have worked in the automotive industry". They finally admitted that.
Those older people who work for General Motors will always have a job because they can be taken care of by a large corporation. General Motors has spent a great deal of money re-educating their electrical maintenance people to become electronic maintenance people. At the present time General Motors maintains that there has been no reduction in staff, but they do acknowledge that, as more robots become available, there will be a reduction in staff. However, the management of General Motors still argues with me. The point to be made here is that the necessity of maintaining the new equipment will almost take up the slack by employing the people who used to put the wheels on the cars.
I would like to see the Government address the social problems of high technology. I would like to have the Government allay the fears the people have of losing their jobs. I would like to see the Government provide some incentive for these people to do other things. Perhaps these other things may be the cottage industry, it may be art, it may be a multitude of different things. We must stress the importance of the individual because the machine will take over by doing what individuals have done in the past.
We must encourage individuals to do more on their own. As long as people have a basic job and can make the same income in two and a half to three days a week that they made in five days in the past, then they can be productive Canadians with other interests. The Government will benefit, because if these
May 6, 1983

other interests develop on a commercial basis they would then be taxed by the federal Government.
Basically, the economy is nothing more than a great big machine. Every time the wheel goes around in this machine, the Government takes a dollar from it. The faster the wheel turns, the more dollars the Government gets. This is important because it would assist in reducing the debt load that our children will be carrying. We have gone through trying times and our debt load is very heavy. When the Keynesian theory has been used in good times, there are no funds in reserve available to attack the social problems of high technology during trying times.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) for his grasp of the major problem that technology will bring about in the human dimension. In light of what he has told us, I think it is important to go back and look at other periods of time in which the same kind of maximum shift occurred to see what is necessary to retain from the former style of life and what is no longer necessary to retain.
I think an example of this is the steamship industry. Although I am a prairie boy and have never been in close proximity to ships, I have always been fascinated by boats and ships on the oceans. As I have travelled around the world I have seen all of the different shapes and styles of sailing ships.
I think it took about 8,000 years to develop a four-masted clipper that could go to any part of the world. I have often wondered what the people who sailed on the clippers thought when they first saw a steamship. It had taken 8,000 years to make this machine of wood, cloth, steel and whatever was necessary. Then someone came along with the steamboat, and the clipper might as well have been 3,000 years old. People who sailed clippers had something to offer those who sailed steamships. They had the experience of the seas. They knew the tides, they knew how to navigate and they knew how to dock. They had an abundance of experience which was beneficial to those who operated steamboats. Perhaps they could not make the transition into the steamboat era, but nevertheless they had something to leave with steamboat operators.
I would like to indicate one problem to the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) which could be brought about by the new technology. It could be difficult to retain the old values which I think are important in society, such as the human values. When we look at technological change and education, how to use a computer or how to work a new machine, perhaps many of the elements which hold society together will be forgotten. How will the human, ethical or moral dimension be carried on as we go through this new wave of development?

Mr. Speaker, the question of the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was an extremely important one in the whole change or shift in the wave of technology. It is important for society to look at the way families and individuals were actually cared for as each wave
went ahead. In the pre-industrial age the family group was looked at in one way. Prior to that tribal societies were looked at in another way. It was only in the industrial age that the income one would receive from a job became a way to look after a family.
As more and more people do not have jobs-and I do not have the exact answer-a distribution system will have to be found so that everyone will have enough on which to live even though they do not necessarily gain it from a job. Perhaps the definition of a job will have to be changed drastically from the one we now use, as a place to go and spend eight hours. speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Lang (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining this debate let me indicate first that a year or two ago we would not have heard any discussion in the House concerning the technological revolution despite the fact that it had been taking place for approximately ten years. The Japanese have been very involved in studying the technological revolution and indicated their formal investigation and research into the matter in the Mitsubi Report of 1973. This is one of the reasons the Japanese in the 1970s became one of the dominant economies of the world.
As many Hon. Members have pointed out, we are in a very historical period. We are entering the third industrial revolution. As an NDP Member pointed out, the first industrial revolution occurred when we went from an agricultural society to a society of steam engines, an industrial society, at which point 90 per cent of Canadians working in the agricultural sector lost their jobs. Those people who lost their jobs on farms went on to gain new jobs in the cities. These were jobs in the manufacturing sector or in industry in general. If we could put ourselves back into that time when Canadian society and the world society were basically agricultural, we could again sit here and be frightened about the prospects of job displacement or the fact that 90 per cent of the jobs would be displaced; or we could look with imagination at and accept the challenges ahead of us, move on and take advantage of the tremendous productivity increase and wealth generation that takes place in an industrial revolution. We have experienced this in the two previous industrial revolutions with the steam engine and then with the combustion engine.
One of the first things we must overcome as Canadians is resistance to the technological revolution. This can be found in Governments, in business, in labour and consumers. The dramatic changes which have been occurring are indeed frightening.
I would like to go from the general to the more specific because, as we attain knowledge and take a closer look, the fear diminishes. One of the biggest problems associated with the industrial revolution, without question, is job displacement
May 6, 1983

and unemployment. We are hearing these days a lot of rhetorical questions and answers, seeking political points in Question Period, about the unemployment situation. Yet I believe most Hon. Members of Parliament, when they are not in the House, recognize that the majority of this unemployment is structural and is due to the technological revolution, and the best way we can handle it is with a concerted, co-operative effort.
We have to deal with some pretty thorny issues and I am going to take the first one head-on; that is, the deficit. I do not know how we can choose a Prime Minister, a Member of Parliament or a provincial legislator and not consider what this person's views are on the deficit. It has become very much a political question. The deficit is increasing, Government spending is increasing, let us have a return to the right, a return to "small c" conservatism. But how will that impact on our response to the technological revolution?
Hon. Members opposite stand up and say we need further tax incentives for research and development; that we cannot destroy our social security system or our Unemployment Insurance system; that we must have more job training, as the Conservative speakers have all indicated; that we must have more retraining; that we must maintain our educational system; that we must maintain one of our most valuable resources, which is not oil but our human resources, by the best health care system in the world. The importance of a healthy population in an industrial revolution is unquestionable, but often times overlooked. However, just the areas which I have outlined now account for well over 70 per cent of the deficit.
So we must deal with the situation of the deficit. Is our deficit something for which we must sacrifice the many programs which all Hon. Members are saying we need to respond to the technical revolution? Or must we put some different perspective on it?
Let us look back at what the deficits were compared to the GNP in the United States and Canada when the first industrial revolution was going on and when the second industrial revolution was going on. Were there massive increases in investment? Were there higher Government deficits and higher business deficits in order to adapt and to modernize the industries in the first and the second industrial revolution? Did that occur? Yes, it did. And if Hon. Members look back at the records they will see that this is the case.
This is also linked with the question of productivity. We have all heard how badly Canada is doing in terms of productivity, if you listen to much of the media or many of the Opposition Members. Quite frankly, that is not the case. We are one of the top five nations in the world in productivity. It is true, however-and I see an Hon. Member shaking his head- that our rate of increase in productivity has been diminishing. This, Mr. Speaker, is something we must address and which this Government has been addressing, particularly in the last budget.
If we look over the medium and long term, we know that with a technological revolution there is a productivity multiplier effect. There is also a wealth generating effect. One of the first problems we must address is how to redistribute this
Supply
wealth in such a way that those workers who have lost their jobs in the more traditional industries are able to obtain retraining in the new kinds of industries which will develop with the technological revolution.
That is not just a pious hope, Mr. Speaker, this is exactly what the Japanese have done. I do not think we can point out often enough that the Japanese have gone through a major portion of a technological revolution without a dramatic increase in unemployment. I believe their unemployment rate is at about 2.9 per cent now. This is not because they have some hidden magic or because they are of a different culture; it is because the Japanese were aware of what was going on when they automated their automobile factories with robotics. They took the workers who were displaced and retrained them for other areas, whether in service, management or marketing, so that they did not have a rapid increase in unemployment. Perhaps they had a better opportunity to do this in their society because it is not quite as pluralistic a society as ours, and it is not quite so free a society as ours. We must face the fact that in Canada we have a number of disadvantages in terms of two levels of Government, a federal and a provincial Government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: We cannot avoid that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
As the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, we cannot avoid that. But what we can do is make sure, through the political will of all of us, that our politicians and our Governments are working in a co-operative manner. And there have been some signs of that, Mr. Speaker. I was very encouraged to note that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) presented his budget, the Treasurer of Ontario, Mr. Frank Millier, indicated that when he brought down his own budget it would be along the same lines, stressing tax incentives for the private sector to enable it to adapt to the technological revolution and to create jobs. I believe that was a very positive note because this was a co-operative effort by different political Parties involved in two different levels of Government.
Another reality which we must face in Canada is the fact that we have for at least 100 years operated on the confrontational or adversarial system, not only in our Governments but between the main economic players in our society. It is not new to say that labour, management, business, Government, all have operated on an adversarial-confrontational system, and it has worked pretty well. However, we can no longer go on in this fashion, Mr. Speaker, or we will be left behind, particularly since we are a competitive trading nation and one-third of our GNP depends upon trade.
What are some of the things which Governments, business, and labour can do? First, if the priority is still "We are going to get as much money as we can without regard to productivity increases, without regard to the viability of the company", then that adversarial position will not be of benefit to labour in negotiating contracts. However, if labour says: "What we really want now is job security, job retraining; these are the

May 6, 1983
Supply
things we are going to bargain for and any increase in wages will be based on increased productivity", then labour will be striking a very positive note.
However, if this does not occur, we already know what will happen. We will have increased unemployment as businesses, particularly multinationals, are able to lay off workers in Canada and use the goods produced by workers who are willing to work for cheaper wages in other countries in the world, particularly in the Third World and in the developing countries.
What about business? Well, business can make a contribution as well. Many businessmen are saying in their interventions that the biggest thing they can take on is innovation of new products, adopting new marketing strategies, the developing of new markets as we come out of the recession. They can take the responsibility of helping to increase productivity through modernization and not blame lack of productivity on labour unions. In short, a co-operative effort.
I have seen this occur in my riding, Mr. Speaker, under the ILAP Program, where industry, labour and Government work together not only to modernize plants but to expand them. The Government's contribution was simply to offer interest-free loans for 50 per cent of capital expenditures for expansion and modernization in the manufacturing and processing field. With that incentive, the business and labour leaders in the Kitchen-er-Waterloo area formed a local ILAP committee and assessed various projects which came forward from both business and labour. We had dramatic increases in the number of jobs created and we had 16 plants modernize or expand in the space of one year. We are looking forward to more so as to increase the number of jobs.
There are other social consequences of the technological revolution apart from job displacement which have been alluded to by other Members. I am thinking of biotechnology where various strains of bacteria produce insulin, or other such genetic manipulation. What are some of the social consequences? Some people fear that these bacteria will get out of control. There might be an accident in the laboratory and a strain of bacteria is developed which is infectious to human beings. Government's responsibility here is to set down certain regulations and guidelines in co-operation with the scientific community so that people can be reasured that with this rapidly changing technology, as with others, we are not endangering the health and safety of our population.
Another example of the social consequences of the technological revolution is a very general one and it comes about so gradually that we may tend to miss it. There is a dramatic increase in stress which we all as individuals feel in a rapidly changing society. There is no question, as Dr. Hans Selye, world renowned expert on stress and a Canadian, has indicated, that the major stress inducing factor is change. We have a rapidly changing society and that will continue with the technological revolution. What is Government's responsibility
here? I think we as representatives of the people must first of all recognize the problem.
Secondly, we should not be so hesitant and concerned when we see jobs in the service sector increasing. This is probably what should be occurring. Stress has a myriad of effects on people, anything from psychosomatic illness such as ulcers to social illnesses. I am thinking of alcoholism, drug addiction, and abuse of various chemicals which we take for granted in our society, such as coffee. Drinking one or two cups of coffee a day is fine, but when we begin drinking seven, eight, nine or ten cups of coffee a day as we adapt to increasing stress, it has a dramatic effect on some of us. People are becoming aware of the problems resulting from too much caffeine. The point I want to make is that there is an increasing amount of stress brought on by technological change.
I would like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by addressing the particulars of the Opposition motion which says the Government is not spending enough on R and D. I take exception to this. I point out to the Opposition that if we stress R and D expenditure as the major aspect of the technological revolution, we are missing the boat. For example, there is no evidence that increased R and D expenditures in the areas of the natural or applied sciences will be the be-all and end-all solution. If we look at the way the Japanese have adapted to the technological revolution, they have used a system of adaption and innovation of existing products. We have seen them do this with many industries where the United States was ahead 20 years ago and the Japanese have come in, taken a look at the products, adapted and moved ahead.
I see you are rising, Mr. Speaker; thank you.

We did not have the Pac-Man, the Atari, the Intellevision, or any of the computer games which are so normal and natural today. I suppose I must conclude that the olden days when I went to school, in the 1960s, will seem much more ancient and old to my son when he reaches my age than it seems to me when I consider the time when my father went to school, in the 1920s and 1930s.
This is because we are going through a society of very rapid change. That is the real world out there, and I think this nation must realize it.
