Instead of typing classes, we now have keypunching classes and others of that sort. That is the real world we are in.
The Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell) spoke very well. I think we must consider the new society as being one which can give us some more hope as human beings, one concerning which we can take a very optomistic point of view, and one which can really be used to liberate human beings from some of the drudgery and work which we have had to do ever since civilization began. That must be the goal and the objective.
At the same time, I think that we must be aware of some of the realities of what is happening. Many of the jobs with which we have been familiar are not there any longer and will not be there in the future. We must ensure that we start retraining people in this country as they are being retrained in other countries around the world so that they are not the victims of technological change. Instead of being its victims, they should be the people who benefit from technological change.
I want to review a few things that are happening in the real world. In the United States, for example, only 3 per cent of the people now work in farming as farmers. Only 13 per cent of Americans now work as blue collars workers in manufacturing plants. Sixty per cent of North Americans work in the information society. Be they teachers, lawyers, accountants, people working in high-tech or with computers, software, hardware or
microelectronics, those Americans working in the so-called information society amount to 60 per cent of the population, with only 13 per cent in manufacturing and 3 per cent in agriculture. The 13 per cent in manufacturing will not increase, no matter which political party is in power, but, rather, will decrease in all industrialized countries around the world. It will decrease the same as it did in agriculture a number of years ago.
My father and my grandfathers before him were farmers in the prairies. In those days, there was a farmer on every quarter section of land on the prairies. I remember the stories that I was told as a child when the farmers would have huge crews of 20 or 30 men at threshing time who would use threshing machines and hay racks. The stooking crews would thrash the grain. Today, that is done by one person with a combine. About 120 years ago approximately 60 per cent of North Americans were working on farms and in agriculture. Today that number is 3 per cent but those 3 per cent produce more than the 60 per cent did some 100 years ago.
The same thing is happening now in manufacturing, mining and many other resource and other industries which have employed so many people over the years. In fact, that change began long ago in 1956. That was the first year that the United States had more people employed in white collar jobs than blue collar jobs. That was almost 30 years ago. When the Russians launched the first Sputnik satellite that orbited the world in 1957, it was a sensational way of opening up the world to the information society.
I believe we are undergoing very rapid changes. I have three deep and genuine concerns about what we should be doing as policy-makers in light of this reality. First, the Science Council of Canada said as recently as two days ago that our country is not keeping up with other countries in the world in terms of advanced technology, equipment, machinery and devices. The Council has said that we are about five years behind smaller countries in western Europe. That is half of a decade, which is far more significant than 30 or 40 years ago. We were told that we are spending less on R and D than other less industrialized countries. While we will be spending $700 million on advanced technology over the next two years, other countries such as France, Germany, Britain and the Scandinavian countries are spending billions of dollars.
We should also be aware of the fact that Canada is already far behind in terms of our trade deficit in high technology. In 1982 our net trade deficit was $8 billion in high technology. Many of the computers and office equipment that we import from abroad could be produced here in Canada. We do not produce the silicon chip in Canada even though we use so many of them every day in our nation. In fact, when one speaks to those in the computer industry they will say that if we do not change our ways our trade deficit in computers alone by 1990 will be some $10 billion in Canada. Imagine the
May 6, 1983

loss of jobs, wealth and economic activity that this means to Canadians, particularly young people who are fully capable of being trained in this country to build chips, computers and other microelectronic equipment that we are and will be using in Canada.
Today, our society is one in which soon every child will have a computer on his desk in every classroom in the country, but we will be importing those computers from abroad. That shows a lack of foresight and planning and is a disgrace to a country as talented as ours.
A second concern I have is that of the little high technology industry that does exist in this country, 40 per cent is already foreign owned and controlled. Many Canadian firms are now very vulnerable to foreign takeovers. Whatever industry we do have in Canada will end up like the oil industry today, being foreign owned, if we do not take appropriate action. The situation may even be worse since there will not be branch plants in the country. Instead we will be importing all of the high-tech equipment for our country's use. We must become aware of these realities as a nation and have some vision and confidence.
I am also concerned about the transition from our industrial society to our information society and how it affects so many people by unemployment. While I do not believe anyone has all the answers, one solution is obviously retraining. Perhaps we will move into a society in which we will continue to have shorter work weeks. We began some years ago with a 65-hour work week and we are now down to 40-hour work weeks. Perhaps there will be 15 or 20-hour work weeks in our society 50 years from now and we will have five or six weeks of holidays instead of three or four weeks. The Government of Francis Mitterrand is now experimenting with shortening the work week from 40 hours to 35 hours.

speechtext:
Suddenly my Conservative friends get very upset. They are afraid to look at any new and different ideas. I suggest that they will have to consider the possibility of continuing to shorten the work day or work week and increasing the holiday time in the years ahead. I say that because many of the jobs today will disappear and we will have to take care of those displaced people fairly and equally, whether my friends in the Liberal Party like it or not.
Let me use the automobile industry as an example. Last September, I had the opportunity to speak in Chicago to the United Auto Workers. The director of research of the American United Auto Workers told the convention that even if the United States retrieved its full share of auto production from the Japanese and others, only 17 years from now, in the year 2000, 80 per cent of the jobs that existed in the booming 1970s will have disappeared because of robotics and the fully automated factory.
There are now automobile factories in Japan in which 98 per cent of the operation is robotized. The average time for producing a car in Japan is some 11 hours, while it is some 31 hours in the United States. Robots in Japan are now producing cars in nine hours. The cost in terms of robots is about $5 an
Supply
hour, whereas in terms of human labour the cost is $15 an hour for salary and benefits. This is the reality. As legislators we will have to consider ways to retrain workers who are displaced rather than letting them simply draw Unemployment Insurance or go on welfare. That is the challenge we face and we must ensure that the ordinary people are not the victims of the robots.
We are heading toward a robotized society in the world. The Japanese now have plants in which robots are building robots. In fact, in a machine plant just outside of Tokyo there are robots working the nightshift with only one human in the plant, the night watchman. That is the type of society that is evolving in our world.
I strongly suggest that we begin to retrain our people and put more money into upgrading their skills and preparing them for the world of today and tomorrow. The Japanese have 40 times as many young people in electrical engineering schools as we do in Canada and Japan has five times our population. Other countries such as Germany, France, Austria and Scandinavian countries put more emphasis on retraining than we do in Canada, and as a result the unemployment rate is lower and the standard of living is higher.
I believe that today's society also causes us to raise many questions about the direction in which our country is headed. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) raised the question of our human values and the concept of our moral issues in terms of the machine and human beings. I think they were very good questions. We are moving into a society where many of the things we took for granted years ago, such as the value of physical labour and the value of capital, are being challenged. We are now entering into a society in which perhaps information is more important and brain intensive industries will be more important, where the knowledge that one possesses will be key in determining whether an industry is efficient or productive. I think a lot of the theories we had in the past are now being challenged.
It is important in this new revolution that we maintain very human values of sharing, co-operating and building and that we use high technology and new innovations to liberate people to make sure that we are not the slaves of the robot, that we make the robot work for us. We should make sure that we use technology to eliminate jobs that are dangerous in terms of health and safety and eliminate jobs that are jobs of drudgery. We should use the new technology to increase our productivity so that we will have more wealth to go around, to give human beings more free time and time to do work in the human and social field than has been done in the past. If we do that, then we can create a society that is better and more decent in the years that lie ahead.
Because of the new technologies we have a chance to have a more decentralized or a more democratic society as well. It will be a more flexible society. We should try to use these new

May 6, 1983
Supply
tools to make sure that does happen and we do not continue building bigger and bigger cities that are more and more polluted. Nor should we continue building more and more expressways. Instead we should have a more balanced growth in our society and promote more self-reliance, encourage more economic democracy, so that the ordinary people have more say over their lives and their environment than has been the case in the past.
I do think these are some of the things that can be accomplished. These are some of the things that we will have to think seriously about as legislators.
I have tried to raise a number of questions this afternoon. I do not know what the answers are to many of the issues we have been discussing today. I do think the values and objectives of a humane and decent society must remain. We must use the new technology, the robots and computers, to enhance that humaneness and decency and to try to increase the standard of living of the poor and the dispossessed. If we can do that, then surely the world of the twenty-first century can be a lot more just and exciting than the world we are experiencing right now.

Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has just described very adequately the problems resulting from the introduction of robotics in the '80s. He compared this problem with the dilemma Western societies were faced with after the war due to automation which replaced a labour force which was unable to adjust. He mentioned also the need to retrain and upgrade the skills of our labour force. Would he not agree with me, however-I think I gathered from his remarks that he favours the development of higher-technology and robotics-when I say that in the long run, according to the experts, robots will create new jobs, just as automation did. However, in the short run, we will be faced with a rather serious unemployment situation which will affect especially the non-skilled workers who, no matter what program we may implement, will be displaced by robots. This will create in our society a fairly high level of unemployment which will add to the unemployment with which we are already faced today.

Yes Mr. Speaker.
I have been an optimist for a long time. I believe that in the long run, there will be more jobs available in Canada, provided we establish a high technology development policy. Last year, unfortunately, for lack of such a policy, we had an international trade deficit of approximately $8 billion in the field of high technology and several countries have now out distanced us. I
for one believe that there will be an increasing reliance on computers in schools for example as well as in all sectors of society.
I just read an article by an American economist which stated that by 1985, 75 per cent of all jobs in North America will require the use of a computer.
In my opinion, it makes a lot of sense to have a high technology sector in Canada. It is crucial that we in Canada manufacture computers and all the goods that we need in this country. It is very important in order to avoid relying too often on imports.
The problem must be addressed immediately. We have to cope with the transition from today's world to the society in which we will line 15 or 20 years from now. That is the issue and I believe that the challenge for us, as members of Parliament, is to find a way, through retraining programs like those in Japan or in European countries to provide new jobs for Canadians.

speechtext: In his intervention, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) described some of the difficulties experienced by Governments which are literally assaulted by the great many calls for help from declining industries in a world of high technology. Given our limited budgetary resources, I would like to ask him to what extent he is suggesting that we, as a Government and as elected Members, help high technology industries-which will necessarily reduce our assistance to declining industries-and what will be the impact in terms of unemployment and jobs in those lagging industries which are generally rather labour intensive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a very thorny and very important issue.
I think that Canada can have a lot of economic changes. We have spent quite a bit of money to build the F-18, for instance, and a lot more as well for useless things. I would suggest that we must do as many other countries of the world have done, including Japan, France, the Federal Republic of Germany and the Scandinavian countries, and that is spend more money on high technology. Recently I called upon Dr. Stuart Smith, the Chairman of the Science Council of Canada, a Government of Canada agency. He often says that many other countries are now ahead of Canada. He also says that, according to the percentage of our GNP, we have spent much less in Canada than many other countries have and that we will have to change our priorities.
That is why the standard of living in Canada has been dropping since 1960 when we ranked second in the world, whereas we are now no higher than 18th or 19th. That is why we have to review our economic priorities. We need an economic strategy for the future.
May 6, 1983

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). He outlined how much more efficient Japan is compared to the U.S.A.; for example, building a car in 11 hours compared to 31. Would the Hon. Member agree with me that the decision of our Government and the U.S. Government in the early 1970s to hold down the price of world energy was a dramatic interference in the world marketplace and that it actually affected us adversely in the sense that we held down the oil price, which sent a signal to our automobile manufacturers to continue to build big cars for us to buy? Meanwhile in Germany and Japan where they had to go to the world price on energy, they immediately turned their top scientific engineers toward producing more efficient cars. Some eight or ten years later they are beating us in the marketplace. Does the Hon. Member agree that that decision by Government interfered with the marketplace to such an extent that it has made our automotive industry out of date today?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 62-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT-NECESSITY FOR FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that may have been one of the factors, but there are many factors why the North American auto industry is behind the auto industry in Japan and Europe. Management in general in North America, in private corporations, tends to be shortsighted. There is too much emphasis on quarterly and annual profits rather than long-term planning. Also, in Europe and Japan greater priority is given to quality products rather than quantity. That is the major difference in the business community between North America, the Japanese and Europeans. The Europeans and Japanese are more concerned with the long term. They might have some short-term losses, but in the long run they want to ensure that they are internationally more competitive.
Our management is very shortsighted. Productivity is basically a management problem. It is management that makes important decisions about technological change or whether to expand certain industries. In North America we tend to have become caught up in the consumer process. We build more and more shopping centres, have more and more kinds of dog food and do more and more things that are basically useless. They do not make that mistake as much in Europe and Japan.
When it comes to research and development the Americans spend a bit more than the Japanese, but not much more. The big difference is that Americans spend about half of their research and development funds on military research and development while the Japanese spend almost zero.
It is very difficult to answer the question directly. It is like comparing apples and oranges. There are many cultural differences. I am being honest; I am not trying to skate away from what the Hon. Member is asking. There are many cultural differences. There are many things we can learn from them about quality of life rather than quantity. Because of the world recession and the fact that some of our resources are running out, hopefully we will put more emphasis on human values.

Mr. Speaker, a motion written in a political environment could hardly praise the Government for what it does. Otherwise, the Opposition would be remiss in its duty. The motion tends to ignore certain developments and initiatives taken by the Government that ought to be put on the record.
The motion seems to indicate that the Government has not dealt with research and development and specialized training. The question of research and development was put forward as recently as three weeks ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in his budget. This was done quite forcefully with substantial measures aimed at promoting, facilitating and creating incentives for the private sector with regard to research and development. That was only three weeks ago. That element ought to have had at least a minimum of recognition in the Hon. Member's motion.
Moving on to specialized training, the motion seems to have been written in a vacuum. For the past ten months this country has been engaged in a massive program of adult training under the auspices of the National Training Act and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). That is an outstanding shortcoming of the motion of the Hon. Member for St. John's East. As I said before, he cannot put forward a motion praising the Government, but by going to the extent of condemning the Government for not having done that which it evidently has done is an approach that is not conducive to putting the facts on the record; perhaps it does elicit a reaction from the Government side of the kind I am providing.

May 6, 1983
Supply
Having said that, I congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East. In a highly political way he has put an important issue on the table. He deserves to be commended for that initiative. His initiative has led to some interesting and thoughtful interventions this afternoon. We had input from the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang), the Hon. Member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell), the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and others. Their comments will be of guidance to the policymakers of this country as to how to approach the question of technological change.
With the inevitable fear that the issue of technological change is creating among Canadians, it would be worthwhile to put on record a quotation that dates back to 1931. The then Director of the International Labour Organization stated that one of the factors in the unemployment program at that time was "the disorganization of the labour market caused by the extra rapid development of labour-saving machinery and the process of rationalization".
We all have to realize the effect of the new processes on the labour market in the eighties which are vastly greater than they were in the thirties. In 1931, Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Director at the Internationl Labour Organization reported, in his evidence of the effects of mechanical improvements on employment, that the agricultural combine deprives five agricultural workers of employment, In Canada the number of such combines increased from two in 1922 to some 7,215 in 1929. In that way a displacement of some 36,000 workers took place over a period of seven years. I doubt, however, whether in the 1980s we will have as much breathing space available as was available in the twenties.
The technological revolution that we are debating here today seems to be embodied in the miniaturized computer which has introduced into the industrial process an element of automation. The problem facing us is not a question of whether the process is good or bad; it is how we handle the process, how we manage it.
It seems to me that the Hon. Member from Yorkton-Melville, in his intervention, put his finger on what seems to me to be the essence of the approach that should be developed. That is that we must consider the effect of technological change on employment, on income distribution, on health and safety, and on labour relations. We can learn how to manage these effects by putting a human face on technological change. If at the center of our concern are the men and women affected by the change, then I believe we will have learned from the agricultural and industrial revolution of past decades and we will have learned the important lessons that those changes taught us to the benefit of present and future generations. This seems to me to be the essence of what this debate is all about.
In 1982 we established a task force on microelectronics and employment. It was conducted by Dr. Margaret Fulton and was completed last November. It was produced in the form of a very concise report entitled "In the CHIPS: Opportunities for Employment". Since then it has been the object of intense consultations with labour and management, because, of course,
the recommendations contained therein touch on these facets of technological change.
We know, Mr. Speaker, that this technological change will affect the pattern of demand for labour. It will probably produce a surplus of unskilled workers and a shortage of skilled workers. It will create a necessity for training of the specialized kind that there is presently under the National Training Act and to which the motion before us makes reference. It will probably have an effect on workers in the service industry, and particularly, I suppose, on office workers. Technological change will probably have an effect on hours of work, on part-time work, on work sharing, and perhaps it will have a considerable effect on the question of early retirement and ways of inducing it and facilitating it for those who wish to take advantage of such possibilities.
On the side of health and safety, Mr. Speaker, technological change could also bring about new hazards, possibly with a greater influence on psychological problems. Therefore, the dangers of technological change in relation to health and safety may not be as evident as they were in the past and it will require greater research to prevent their occurrence.
I would like to express my gratitude to the Member from St. John's East because he has put on the table perhaps the most important issue that faces not only this Government but any Government that has an industrial concern and a labour force that is affected by technological change. This issue is that there will probably have to be greater flexibility in the future on the part of management and labour and that there will have to be some form of partnership developed between labour, management and Governments in the future. It is quite possible that management will have to give up more of its residual rights, become more democratic and encourage forms of co-determination and co-management. We have heard echoes of this from other countries in the past decade and these echoes are now reaching our shores. Maybe labour will have to be reassured so that it can accept the inevitable change. The assurance that should be given to labour is the assurance of some form of job security and employment growth.
This leads me to refer to the budget again as I did a moment ago, because contained in the budget is an important element which some speakers on the opposite side have seemed to overlook, although not all of them have. I regret that I have not heard all of the interventions. This element in the budget is the reference to a centre of productivity and employment growth. That centre is an instrument of a highly technical nature where technological change will be the focus, a forum where business and Government can bring to the fore experience at the shop floor level, as they say, bring to the attention of all the experience of the front line of the workplace in order to find some short-term answers to questions that have been of concern to some of the speakers on the opposite side. Those, of course, are the concerns of the Government as well. Beyond that, evidently answers will have to be found of a medium-term
May 6, 1983

nature and of a long-term nature, and the challenge is now before us.
Through its budget of April 19, 1983 the Government has made an offer to fund a centre if there is the will to create one, a place where labour can play a central role, together with business and with Government, in the shaping of our future, in the managing of this technological change and in the exchange and the bringing together of experiences as seen from different angles, in an attempt to search for solutions. Evidently the solutions are not easy to find and the finding of them cannot be the exclusive domain of one party or the other, of Parliament alone or the Government alone.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that better answers will come as a result of consultations and co-operation by all of the sectors in our society that are affected. Inevitably there will be things that labour knows more about, there will be things that business will understand better, and there will be another range of knowledge and experience that the Government will be able to contribute in the interest of the public at large.
The future lies in these kinds of measures. I suppose the creation of a subcommittee of Cabinet on technology must have been brought up earlier in the debate. Mr. Speaker, what more evidence is needed to demonstrate to you that there has been and there is now forward thinking on the part of this Government of the kind that this Opposition motion does not seem to be aware of or does not want to take into consideration? If these elements that I am submitting for your consideration seem valid to you, the motion before us that condemns the Government has no foundation.
What I do welcome, though, is the fact that this debate has put forward a number of interesting propositions. There have been interesting questions and points raised by the Member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) who made inquiries about the Labour Code earlier this afternoon.
Some interesting questions were asked by Hon. Members concerning the management of change in general. This issue is so important and fundamental to the survival of society and to the benefit of all Canadians that it requires more than just a political, partisan approach, which is understandable within the confines of these four walls. It will require very active and intensive participation and co-operation so as to trigger the input of all interested parties. Therefore, I place a particular importance on the creation of the centre mentioned in the budget of April 19.1 see it as a vehicle to approach these issues which could make a considerable difference.
There are skeptics who say that this country is not ready for an approach by labour, business and Government. I am somewhat saturated, to say the least, with references to Japan and Japanese models. Quite frankly, those models from abroad have their own merits within the confines of those particular cultures. It is important to study them and to learn about their existence but, having done so, we have to turn around, look at ourselves and seek our own identity so that we can implement
Supply
our own ways of doing things. It cannot be the Japanese way or the European way; it has to be the Canadian way.
In this respect I remind Hon. Members that in Canada we have some interesting models which have already been developed. For example, we have an approach through the vehicle of task forces as announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) on several occasions in recent months. There is what could be called a bilateral model in the automotive industry which has a labour leader and a recognized industrial leader working together, co-chairing a task force and producing a report, in the case of the automotive industry, I suppose in the matter of a few weeks. They deliver to Government their findings and conclusions and then leave it to Government to make a decision in the interests of that particular industrial sector and of the public at large. That model is being repeated in the forestry industry. It could be said that somehow it is a continuation of the sectoral approaches of 1978 or thereabouts when some ten or 20 sectors were developed for study as an initiative of the Liberal Government.
Parallel to the bilateral approach we have a trilateral approach which exists in at least four places in Canada, all at the federal level. I will not venture into the provincial level where I am sure there are ongoing trilateral models, particularly in the fields of apprenticeship training and counselling across the board in most Provinces. But at the federal level in Hamilton, for instance, there is the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety run by a council consisting of labour, business and the Government. In Ottawa we have the Labour Adjustment Benefit Board, which is also run by a trilateral body. In addition we have the Export Development Board which advises the Minister in charge of exports and consists of three sectoral individuals representing labour, management and business. Finally we have the Textile Advisory Board-

shown to us indicated the danger of 15 per cent unemployment. One of the reasons we find ourselves in our present position is perhaps because the Government of Canada has forgotten two things. In terms of the size of the deficit, which may be a drag on the economy and on our recovery, it has forgotten the biblical injunction to save in the good years against the bad. It spends, spends, spends in the good years; spends, spends, spends in the bad years; and we have that drag which may very well dampen our recovery.
Second, as Governments will take the benefit to which I think they are entitled when things go reasonably well, they have to take the responsibility when things go reasonably bad. There is no doubt we are suffering today from the fact that Governments have failed to foresee the abvent of the information society and the importance of this new technology. Only now are lights going on when we face some tremendous problems in the community. There is not a supporter of the Government opposite who could honestly rise and say that this is the appropriate time to begin these changes. As a matter of fact, the appropriate time has long since past. That is a tragedy which will be borne by many young people who are now unskilled and will be caught in the short-term period. I do not want anyone in the House to think that there are not some tremendous advantages to the technological change which is now coming about, if we are wise enough to plan for it and to take advantage of it.
Some Members have talked about the changes in the industrial revolution with the invention of the steam engine, such as the change in the agricultural community which resulted in displaced workers. Those workers went to the cities
to find new jobs. The high technology industry is not only developing for itself; it is developing technology to be used in existing industries to upgrade them, to make them more competitive and more productive, to create new jobs and new product lines to improve our place in world markets. We have to be awake and wise enough to take advantage of this. It is the challenge which faces every one of us, but this motion condemns the Government because it is starting awfully late.
I urge Hon. Members of the Government to read a little book entitled "While There is Time", by Stephen Leacock. He had the following to say about Canada in a very short passage:
-Canada is as empty as ever-almost; still abundant room, abundant opportunity, life and all that makes it sweet, waiting here for uncounted millions of people, serene sky and empty plain, and rivers murmuring in the forest-nature's temple, where we crowd and wrangle round the entrances.
That is still the picture of our country if we are prepared to take advantage of those things which are ours, and one of those things is the advent of the information and communication age.
